Mac DeMarco.description: DeMarco's Captured Tracks debut coined the woozy, chorus-pedal 'jizz jazz' sound that defined blog-era slacker rock: loose, warbly guitar lines, half-mumbled vocals and a stoned, unhurried tempo throughout. It set the template for a decade of goofball-slacker singer-songwriters.
Mac DeMarco.lineage: Descends from Pavement's shambling guitar pop and the Flying Nun DIY-jangle tradition; directly influences the 2010s slacker-rock and bedroom-pop wave that followed.

Mac DeMarco.description: DeMarco's best-known record is a warmer, more melodic take on his slacker sound, about the anxieties of encroaching adulthood delivered with a shrug. The title track and 'Passing Out Pieces' became blog-rock standards.
Mac DeMarco.lineage: Refines the '2' blueprint into DeMarco's signature sound; a touchstone for the 2010s jangle/slacker revival.

Mac DeMarco.description: A quieter, more acoustic-leaning record built around fingerpicked guitar and synth textures, dealing with DeMarco's relationship with his father. Still slacker in tone but more reflective than his earlier records.
Mac DeMarco.lineage: Shows the slacker-rock lineage bending toward hushed singer-songwriter territory.

Mac DeMarco.description: Self-released on DeMarco's own label, this record strips his sound to its most repetitive and hypnotic, with simple, mantra-like song structures and titles. A deliberately low-key follow-up that trades hooks for mood.
Mac DeMarco.lineage: DeMarco's move to full DIY self-release, closing the loop back to the Bandcamp/DIY network this lane traces.

Mac DeMarco.description: A wordless, tape-warped song cycle Mac DeMarco pieced together while driving cross-country, all warm Rhodes, brushed drums and looping guitar vamps instead of his usual slack-jawed vocals. It plays like a private travelogue, mixing his usual chorus-pedal haze with lounge and ambient touches. For listeners who want the DeMarco sound stripped of singing.
Mac DeMarco.lineage: Extends the bedroom-pop haze of his Captured Tracks records into instrumental territory, closer to Jim O'Rourke's ambient side than to Pavement.

Mac DeMarco.description: Mac DeMarco's sixth solo album returns to his slack, chorus-drenched pop songwriting after the instrumental detour of Five Easy Hot Dogs, foregrounding sun-warped guitar tone and his familiar half-mumbled melodies. It is unhurried, private-sounding pop built for headphones on a walk. Fans of Salad Days will find the same loose, wobbly charm.
Mac DeMarco.lineage: A return to the vocal jangle-pop songwriting of Salad Days and This Old Dog after an instrumental record, still rooted in his Captured Tracks-era slacker sound.

Macie Stewart.description: A Chicago multi-instrumentalist's (Ohmme, Marker) solo debut: spare piano- and violin-inflected songs recorded mostly alone, moving between chamber-folk intimacy and quiet dissonance.
Macie Stewart.lineage: Grows out of Chicago's overlapping indie-folk/experimental scene, tied to Orindal labelmates Gia Margaret and Macie Stewart's other Chicago projects.

Mae Powell.description: Powell's sophomore album, a jazz-inflected folk-rock record carried by her standout voice and a five-piece band of close friends; immaculate, warm instrumental textures throughout.
Mae Powell.lineage: Bay Area indie-folk/jazz-folk crossover scene; her voice draws comparisons to classic soul and folk singers alike.

Magnolia Electric Co..description: Recorded in Brussels in April 2003 while the band still toured as Songs: Ohia, this live album was the first release under the Magnolia Electric Co. name. Stretched-out versions of songs like 'The Big Beast' lean hard into Crazy Horse-style guitar jams, with reviewers at the time noting the overt Neil Young worship. It is the document of the exact moment Molina's haunted folk band turned into a loud, loose country-rock outfit.
Magnolia Electric Co..lineage: Documents Jason Molina's pivot from the hushed Songs: Ohia sound toward Crazy Horse-scale guitar rock, a move that set the template for Magnolia Electric Co.'s studio albums.

Magnolia Electric Co..description: The first proper studio album under the Magnolia Electric Co. name, recorded with Steve Albini at Electrical Audio, pairs Molina's cracked baritone with a full touring band for the first time. Songs like 'Northstar Blues' and 'Give Something Else Away Every Day' move at a slow, heavy backbeat, closer to a bar-band Crazy Horse than the spare folk of earlier Songs: Ohia records. It reads as a bridge record, still carrying some of the older band's hush but built for a road-worn rock lineup.
Magnolia Electric Co..lineage: Extends Songs: Ohia's haunted folk into full-band country rock, cementing the Magnolia Electric Co. sound that Will Johnson's Centro-matic and South San Gabriel records run parallel to.

Magnolia Electric Co..description: Assembled from four separate sessions -- including one produced by Cracker's David Lowery in Richmond and one at Sun Studio in Memphis -- 'Fading Trails' is patchier and more fragmentary than its predecessor, mixing full-band rockers like 'Don't Fade on Me' with short, spare pieces like 'Montgomery'. All of its songs later resurfaced in fuller form on the 'Sojourner' box set. It captures Molina restlessly moving between studios and lineups in the years before Magnolia Electric Co. wound down.
Magnolia Electric Co..lineage: A transitional Magnolia Electric Co. record whose sessions were later collected whole on the 'Sojourner' box set, showing Molina's late-2000s method of recording in pieces across different studios and bands.

Magnolia Electric Co..description: A limited wooden box set collecting three full albums (including the otherwise-unreleased 'Nashville Moon', produced by Steve Albini), a four-song EP, and a tour documentary, all drawn from the same 2005-2007 sessions that fed 'Fading Trails'. Because it gathers complete, otherwise-hard-to-find recordings rather than just repackaging an existing album, it functions as a genuine (if sprawling) entry in the discography rather than a reissue. It is for the committed listener who wants the full session-by-session picture of Magnolia Electric Co.'s mid-2000s work.
Magnolia Electric Co..lineage: Collects the same 2005-2007 Magnolia Electric Co. sessions that produced 'Fading Trails' in their entirety, including material otherwise unavailable, and stands as the fullest document of the band's road-band, Crazy Horse-indebted period.

Magnolia Electric Co..description: Recorded quickly with Steve Albini as a tribute to Magnolia Electric Co. bassist Evan Farrell, who died in 2009, 'Josephine' is the band's last studio album released in Molina's lifetime. It is quieter and more mournful than the road-band records around it, built on hushed strumming and Molina's weathered voice on songs like the title track and 'Whip-poor-will'. It works as a fitting, restrained close to the Magnolia Electric Co. catalog.
Magnolia Electric Co..lineage: Closes out Magnolia Electric Co.'s studio catalog as a memorial record for bassist Evan Farrell, recorded just before Molina's final years of illness and his one collaboration with Will Johnson.

Major Murphy.description: A cohesive, jittery-warm record of jangle-pop songwriting, praised by Katie Crutchfield for its full-album craft. Grand Rapids band mixing heavy rock'n'roll textures with pop hooks.
Major Murphy.lineage: Descends from Big Star/Flying Nun jangle-pop songwriting via the Midwest DIY circuit.

Major Murphy.description: Grand Rapids trio Major Murphy follows Access with eight songs that add strings for the first time, weaving classic-rock and vintage soft-rock touches into their usual blend of 1990s indie looseness and 1970s AM-radio warmth. It's their most psychedelic and emotionally direct record about parenthood and creative life.
Major Murphy.lineage: Extends Major Murphy's own hybrid of 1990s indie rock and 1970s soft-rock songwriting established on Access, in the lineage of Big Star's more orchestrated moments.

Mali Velasquez.description: I'm Green is Mali Velasquez's folk-inflected indie rock debut, nine songs that swing between hushed verses and explosive choruses. Her plainspoken lyrics and warm voice place her alongside a wave of songwriters bridging bedroom folk and full-band indie rock.
Mali Velasquez.lineage: A fresh voice in the same lane as Katy Kirby, working the space between quiet acoustic folk and full-band indie rock.

Maneka.description: Devin McKnight's third Maneka album sits at the combustible intersection of slowcore and shoegaze, alternating quiet, acoustic reflection with head-splitting noise. Engineer Alex Farrar's production keeps the extremes cohesive.
Maneka.lineage: McKnight (formerly of Speedy Ortiz and Grass Is Green) built Maneka as a showcase for genre-crossing songwriting; this album's slowcore passages place it squarely in this lane alongside Horse Jumper of Love and Joyer.

Mapache.description: Clay Finch and Sam Blasucci's duo debut is built on intertwined nylon and steel-string acoustic guitars and close, easy harmonies, closer to Everly Brothers or Simon & Garfunkel than jam-band sprawl. It is unhurried, warm California folk-country, intimate rather than expansive.
Mapache.lineage: Rooted in Laurel Canyon duo harmony singing and 1970s California country rock, feeding directly into the Beachwood Sparks-adjacent scene that includes Silver Synthetic and Farmer Dave Scher.

Mapache.description: The duo's major-imprint debut sharpens the songwriting while keeping the same easygoing intertwined-guitar sound, drawing overt inspiration from the Flying Burrito Brothers and classic California country rock. It is warmer and more fully arranged than their debut, without losing its front-porch intimacy.
Mapache.lineage: Continues Mapache's Laurel Canyon-via-California-country lineage with a bigger studio budget and outside collaborators.

Mapache.description: Mapache's third album keeps refining their duo-guitar-and-harmony formula, drawing comparisons to Allah-Las and other West Coast revivalists. It is short, warm and unpretentious, songs built for a porch or a campfire rather than a festival stage.
Mapache.lineage: A continuation of Mapache's steady development of the California cosmic-country duo sound.

Mapache.description: An 18-song, hour-long set of earnest, classic songwriting named for the band's dog, with covers of 'Love Can't Hold Me' and 'Light My Fire' folded into the sprawl. As Josh Terry noted, it is an unpretentious road-trip record from a duo comfortable with letting songs breathe.
Mapache.lineage: The most expansive entry in Mapache's catalog, extending their duo-harmony format across a double-LP-length set.

Mapache.description: A relaxed, well-loved set that includes a cover of the Flying Burrito Brothers' 'Hot Burrito No. 2' alongside originals like 'French Kiss', continuing the duo's front-porch harmony sound with a slightly fuller band arrangement.
Mapache.lineage: Extends Mapache's ongoing homage to Flying Burrito Brothers-style California country rock.

Maple Glider.album: To Enjoy Is the Only Thing
Maple Glider.description: Tori Zietsch's debut as Maple Glider, produced by Tom Iansek, takes inspiration from vignettes of her life and travel in spare, intimate folk songs.
Maple Glider.lineage: Grew from Zietsch's earlier duo project Seavera into a solo folk career on Pieater/Partisan.

Maple Glider.description: Emotionally devastating songs about religion, bodily autonomy and trauma, in the same territory as Julia Jacklin's Pre Pleasure.
Maple Glider.lineage: Second album, continuing Maple Glider's confessional Australian indie-folk songwriting.

Margaux.description: Unfussy yet ornate indie folk-rock ranging from stripped melancholy to lush grooves, from the songwriter who also plays bass in Katy Kirby's band.
Margaux.lineage: Part of the same Brooklyn indie-folk/rock circle as Katy Kirby and Lindsay Reamer.

Margo Price.description: Recorded at Sun Studio and funded by pawning her wedding ring and car, Price's debut is unvarnished honky-tonk about poverty, a lost farm, and the death of an infant son, sung in a clear, unadorned twang. It arrived on Jack White's Third Man Records as a jolt of classic-sounding country amid Music Row's pop-country moment. The foundational document of her career.
Margo Price.lineage: Directly channels Loretta Lynn and Tammy Wynette-style honky-tonk confessional songwriting into the 2010s outlaw revival.

Margo Price.description: Price widens her scope from personal hard-luck stories to overtly political songwriting about gender pay gaps and American hypocrisy, with a Willie Nelson duet ('Learning to Lose') as centerpiece. The arrangements add horns and more classic-rock muscle to the honky-tonk base. A more ambitious, outward-looking sophomore record.
Margo Price.lineage: Extends her honky-tonk foundation toward the socially conscious outlaw-country tradition of Merle Haggard and Loretta Lynn's message songs.

Margo Price.description: Produced by Sturgill Simpson, this record leans further into 1970s arena and soft rock than pure country, with synth textures and bigger choruses. It's Price at her most classic-rock-indebted, trading some twang for widescreen production. A pivot point that shows the 'new outlaw' scene's comfort blurring into rock.
Margo Price.lineage: Shows the same Simpson-produced pivot toward rock textures that also marked Sound & Fury, pulling the neo-traditional scene toward 1970s Southern rock.

Margo Price.description: Written partly after a psychedelic mushroom trip, Strays is Price's most rock-oriented and loosest record, moving between swaggering guitar rock and hazy, druggy ballads. It keeps her plainspoken lyric voice while stretching the arrangements furthest from her honky-tonk roots. For listeners who prefer her rock side to her Sun Studio side.
Margo Price.lineage: Continues the classic-rock drift of That's How Rumors Get Started, pushing further from honky-tonk toward Southern psychedelic rock.

Margo Price.description: A return toward Price's country foundation after two rock-leaning records, built around plainspoken songs about aging, motherhood, and holding a marriage together on the road. It splits the difference between the twang of Midwest Farmer's Daughter and the widescreen arrangements of her later work. Listed among Josh Terry's 2025 longlist without further comment.
Margo Price.lineage: Circles back toward the honky-tonk core of her debut after the rock detours of Strays and That's How Rumors Get Started.

Marina Allen.description: Allen's Chris Cohen-produced follow-up to Candlepower is timeless, classic-songwriting-lineage folk anchored by her mesmerizing, wide-ranging voice.
Marina Allen.lineage: Los Angeles songwriter whose delicate, literary folk songwriting places her alongside Weyes Blood and Cate Le Bon's circle.

Marisa Anderson.description: Anderson plays every instrument on this self-produced record, moving between electric guitar, lap steel, pedal steel, electric piano and percussion to build what she has described as a soundtrack for an imaginary science-fiction Western. It leaves the acoustic blues-and-hymn vocabulary of her earlier records for a spacier, more electric palette without losing the plainspoken, unhurried phrasing that marks all her playing. It is one of the clearest bridges between American Primitive guitar and ambient instrumental music.
Marisa Anderson.lineage: Anderson's background in blues and old-time guitar runs through John Fahey and Sandy Bull's drone-and-raga lineage, and this record's electric widescreen sound anticipates William Tyler's and Chuck Johnson's own moves toward ambient instrumental texture.

Marisa Anderson.description: Anderson's Thrill Jockey debut returns to a more acoustic, blues- and gospel-rooted sound, its steel-string pieces built from slide guitar figures and hymn-like repetition. The playing is patient and unadorned, closer in spirit to Fahey's early Takoma records than to the electric sprawl of Into the Light. It confirmed Anderson as one of the strongest solo-guitar voices to emerge from the 2010s American Primitive revival.
Marisa Anderson.lineage: A deliberate return to the acoustic blues-and-hymn foundation of Fahey's early work after the electric detour of Into the Light, placing Anderson alongside Daniel Bachman and Chuck Johnson in Thrill Jockey's 2010s fingerstyle roster.

Marisa Anderson.description: Made during a period of loss and lockdown isolation, Still, Here is Anderson's most spacious and inward record, its pieces built from long-held tones and simple, repeated phrases that let silence do as much work as notes. It continues her move away from technical display toward mood and space, closer to minimalism than to Fahey's ragtime-inflected picking. The record's stillness reflects its origins as music made for herself before it was made for an audience.
Marisa Anderson.lineage: Continues Anderson's arc toward spare, meditative solo guitar begun on Cloud Corner, part of a broader early-2020s turn toward slow, minimal instrumental guitar shared with Hayden Pedigo and Eli Winter.

Marissa Nadler.album: Songs III: Bird on the Water
Marissa Nadler.description: Nadler's third album pairs her reverb-drenched, ghostly soprano with fingerpicked acoustic guitar and occasional strings, its murder-ballad and gothic-romance imagery closer to Appalachian folk balladry than to singer-songwriter confessionalism. 'Diamond Heart' and 'Mexico' move at a glacial pace, closer in tempo to slowcore than upbeat folk-pop. It is where Nadler's signature hazy, old-time-adjacent sound first fully crystallized.
Marissa Nadler.lineage: Draws on old-time murder ballads and British folk balladry in the vein of early Gillian Welch, slowed and reverbed into a gothic, slowcore-adjacent register distinct from the rest of the lane.

Marissa Nadler.description: Nadler adds a full band and occasional piano and synthesizer here, without losing the reverb-soaked, mournful atmosphere of her earlier records. 'Rats' and 'Mary Come Alive' keep her gothic-ballad character sketches while the arrangements grow slightly fuller and more layered. It sits as a transitional record between her earliest, sparest work and the more accessible songwriting of her 2010s albums.
Marissa Nadler.lineage: A fuller-band continuation of Songs III's hazy, old-time-adjacent balladry, keeping Nadler in the same gothic-folk lane distinct from more upbeat 2000s indie folk.

Marissa Nadler.description: Written after a breakup and produced by Randall Dunn (Sunn O))), Earth), July is Nadler's most widely acclaimed record, its reverb-heavy, slow-motion folk arrangements given cleaner, more deliberate production than her earlier DIY-adjacent albums. 'Was It a Dream' and 'Dead City Emily' keep her gothic balladry but sound more assured and less lo-fi. It charted on both the US and UK folk charts, her commercial high point to that date.
Marissa Nadler.lineage: The clearest, best-produced statement of the slow, reverb-drenched old-time balladry Nadler had developed since Songs III, bridging indie folk and the slowcore lane it borders.

Mark Eitzel.description: Eitzel's first proper solo album after American Music Club's split leans toward jazzy, late-night piano and brushed-drum arrangements, a quieter and more lounge-adjacent setting for his weary voice than any AMC record attempted. The songs keep the slow tempos and downcast lyrics intact while trading Vudi's guitar textures for a more cabaret-like backing band. It is often held up as the strongest of Eitzel's many solo records, a showcase for a voice built entirely around understatement.
Mark Eitzel.lineage: Carries American Music Club's sadcore songwriting into a solo, more torch-song-inflected register, part of the same San Francisco lineage that runs through Red House Painters and Tarnation.

Mark Olson and Victoria Williams.description: After leaving the Jayhawks, Mark Olson and his wife Victoria Williams recorded this desert-folk debut at home in Joshua Tree with a loose collective of friends. It's hushed, harmony-rich country-folk built on acoustic guitars and warm, communal singing, far more homespun than Olson's Jayhawks work. A foundational record for the loose Joshua Tree desert-folk scene that fed the 2000s cosmic-country/Americana revival.
Mark Olson and Victoria Williams.lineage: Grew directly out of Mark Olson's departure from the Jayhawks and Victoria Williams's Americana songwriting; the Creekdippers' communal, desert-recorded sound anticipated the 2010s cosmic-country/Cosmic American Music revival.

Marshall Crenshaw.description: A Detroit songwriter with a deep Buddy Holly fixation, Crenshaw's debut pairs plain, unfussy guitar pop with some of the cleverest, most economical songwriting of the early-1980s power-pop wave. "Someday, Someway" became a minor hit, but the whole record's mix of rockabilly twang and Byrds-descended jangle is remarkably consistent. It is often cited as the purest distillation of early-1960s pop songcraft filtered through a post-punk sensibility.
Marshall Crenshaw.lineage: Extends the Buddy Holly/Byrds/Beatles hook lineage into the early-1980s American power-pop scene, standing alongside Big Star and the dB's as a critics'-favorite entry in the same tradition.

Marty Robbins.description: A concept record of Western narrative ballads, built around the galloping Spanish-guitar riff and murder-ballad plot of 'El Paso,' which crossed over to number one on both country and pop charts. Robbins sings these cowboy-outlaw stories with a clean, theatrical baritone over spare Nashville session backing, treating each song as a short story with a beginning, middle and violent end. AllMusic has called it the most influential Western-ballads album of the postwar era.
Marty Robbins.lineage: Its story-song format and Western imagery fed directly into the outlaw-country movement's cowboy mythology and into narrative country songwriting generally, an explicit reference point for storytelling-heavy Southern rock and alt-country writers who followed.

Marty Stuart.description: After years as a sideman for Lester Flatt and Johnny Cash, Stuart's MCA debut plants a flag for a rockabilly-edged, rhinestone-and-mandolin version of hard country, opening on the title track's driving Telecaster riff and Western Girls, then the horn-punctuated stomp of Cry Cry Cry, which owes as much to Sun Records rockabilly as to contemporary Nashville. Stuart's own bluegrass mandolin chops surface throughout even as the tempos stay closer to rock and roll than to honky-tonk shuffle. It set the template, hillbilly roots played with rock and roll energy and showmanship, that he would keep refining for the rest of his career.
Marty Stuart.lineage: Carries Stuart's bluegrass and Johnny Cash sideman background (via Flatt and Cash, both R1-adjacent) into a rockabilly-flavored neotraditional record that helped define the genre's late-'80s 'hillbilly rock' strand.

Mary Chapin Carpenter.description: Before her 1990s run of mainstream country-radio hits, Mary Chapin Carpenter made Hometown Girl as a quiet, folk-leaning debut built on plainspoken narrative songs and restrained acoustic arrangements, closer to the coffeehouse folk circuit she came from than to Nashville. This Shirt and the title track show off the observational, detail-driven songwriting that would carry through her whole catalog, even after she became a bigger commercial name. It is the record where her folk-Americana roots are most clearly on display before the pop-country crossover.
Mary Chapin Carpenter.lineage: Grew out of the Washington, D.C. folk club circuit rather than Nashville, and represents the country-folk songwriting Carpenter drew on before her 1990s move toward mainstream country radio.

Mary Lou Lord.description: A former Boston subway busker's only major-label album, pairing her plainspoken, slightly nasal voice with jangly folk-rock arrangements and songs co-written with Nick Saloman (the Bevis Frond) and Freedy Johnston. It leans more toward '90s college-radio jangle-pop than lo-fi slacker rock, closer in spirit to Liz Phair's guest spot on the record.
Mary Lou Lord.lineage: Emerged from the Boston indie/busking scene around Bevis Frond and Elliott Smith (who contributed to her earlier EPs); represents the more polished, radio-adjacent edge of '90s indie jangle.

Mason Proffit.description: Formed by brothers Terry and John Michael Talbot in the Chicago area, Mason Proffit's debut mixes Byrds-indebted pedal steel and harmony singing with pointed antiwar and pro-Native-American songs, giving it a more overtly political edge than most of the Los Angeles country-rock scene. It built a strong Midwest live following without matching that success on record. Two Hangmen became something of an underground anthem.
Mason Proffit.lineage: A Chicago-based band applying Byrds and Burritos-style pedal steel country rock to explicitly political songwriting, extending the sound beyond its Los Angeles home base into the Midwest.

Mason Proffit.description: Mason Proffit's second album keeps the pedal steel and brotherly harmonies of the debut while softening some of its overt political edge in favor of more personal songwriting. It remains a well-regarded but commercially marginal record from the band's Happy Tiger years, before a later move to major labels failed to widen their audience. It is a solid, representative document of the Midwest side of the country-rock boom.
Mason Proffit.lineage: Continues Mason Proffit's Byrds-indebted country-rock sound from their debut, the band's second and final album on the small Happy Tiger label.

Material Issue.description: Chicago trio Material Issue built their major-label debut from years of demos into a tight, hook-dense power-pop record, with "Valerie Loves Me" and "Diane" pairing crunchy guitars with unabashedly catchy choruses. Jim Ellison's songwriting leaned harder into radio-scaled pop hooks than most of the jangle-pop underground, closer to the Knack's directness than Big Star's studio nuance. The title later became the name of a long-running annual power-pop festival, cementing the record's place as a genre touchstone.
Material Issue.lineage: A Chicago entry in the early-1990s power-pop revival alongside Matthew Sweet and Velvet Crush, carrying the Beatles/Byrds hook lineage into a harder-edged alt-rock context.

Matt Sweeney & Bonnie 'Prince' Billy.description: A full collaboration with guitarist Matt Sweeney (Chavez, Zwan), Superwolf pairs Oldham's plainspoken, image-dense lyrics with Sweeney's intricate, winding electric guitar lines, giving the songs a more virtuosic instrumental backbone than most of Oldham's solo work. It is widely regarded as one of the best records either musician has made. A key document of the Drag City circle's collaborative side.
Matt Sweeney & Bonnie 'Prince' Billy.lineage: The first major pairing of Oldham with Matt Sweeney, part of the Drag City Bonnie/Smog circle, later revisited on Superwolves in 2021.

Matt Sweeney & Bonnie 'Prince' Billy.description: A long-awaited sequel to Superwolf, reuniting Oldham with guitarist Matt Sweeney sixteen years later, with Malian guitarist Ahmoudou Madassane and Bombino's rhythm section adding a new, subtly West African-inflected texture to Sweeney's guitar lines. The deadpan plainness of Oldham's singing is unchanged even as the instrumental backdrop widens. A strong late-career document of the Drag City circle's most enduring songwriting partnership.
Matt Sweeney & Bonnie 'Prince' Billy.lineage: Directly continues the 2005 Superwolf collaboration, extending one of the most documented recurring partnerships within the Drag City deadpan school.

Matthew Sweet.description: Written during Sweet's divorce and featuring Television's Richard Lloyd and Robert Quine trading searing guitar leads, Girlfriend pairs raw emotional lyrics with the cleanest, most direct power-pop hooks of the early 1990s. The title track and "I've Been Waiting" show how far Sweet had absorbed Big Star and the Byrds into a confessional singer-songwriter frame. It became the commercial and critical breakthrough that proved the classic jangle-pop sound could still work on alternative radio.
Matthew Sweet.lineage: A Nebraska-born, Athens-and-NYC-schooled songwriter's full synthesis of the Big Star/Byrds lineage, cementing the early-1990s power-pop revival alongside Teenage Fanclub and the Posies.

Matthew Sweet.description: Sweet's fourth album keeps Richard Lloyd's guitar work and the same Big Star-descended melodic core as Girlfriend, but with a slightly harder, more compressed alt-rock edge suited to mid-1990s radio. "Sick of Myself" became his biggest hit, driving home just how mainstream the classic jangle/power-pop sound had become by the mid-1990s. It closes out the commercial peak of Sweet's early run in the same lineage as Girlfriend.
Matthew Sweet.lineage: A continuation of Sweet's Big Star/Byrds synthesis into the mid-1990s, part of the broader power-pop revival that also produced Velvet Crush's Teenage Symphonies to God the year before.

Mazzy Star.description: Hope Sandoval's smoky, drawled vocals and David Roback's reverb-heavy guitar and slide work built a debut that moves like a slow drift through desert psychedelia and Southern gothic blues, closer to a hazy Mazzy Star than to any of that year's noisier LA scene. The tempos rarely rise above a lazy shuffle, and the production leaves plenty of empty space around Sandoval's voice. It grew out of Roback's earlier Rain Parade and Opal projects, carrying Paisley Underground psychedelia into a slower, more hushed register.
Mazzy Star.lineage: Carries Roback's Paisley Underground roots (Rain Parade, Opal) into a slower, more Southern-gothic direction, becoming a key crossover between '60s psych revivalism and '90s slowcore/sadcore.

Mazzy Star.album: So Tonight That I Might See
Mazzy Star.description: Mazzy Star's biggest record pairs the same slow, reverb-soaked formula as the debut with a genuine hit in 'Fade Into You,' whose hushed strings and brushed drums brought the band's slow-motion sound to mainstream radio without changing its essential approach. Elsewhere the record leans into longer, more hypnotic pieces like the ten-minute 'Into Dust,' proving the single was no fluke compromise. Sandoval's voice stays low and unhurried throughout, a constant against Roback's shifting guitar textures.
Mazzy Star.lineage: Brought the slow, drawled, reverb-heavy sadcore sound to a mainstream audience via 'Fade Into You,' widening the genre's visibility well beyond the underground labels most of its peers stayed on.

Mazzy Star.description: The last Mazzy Star album for nearly two decades trades some of the previous record's brighter moments for a darker, more claustrophobic mood, with Sandoval's vocals mixed even further back into Roback's murky guitar and organ arrangements. Tempos stay slow throughout, and the record leans into a more overtly bleak, druggy atmosphere than its predecessors. It did not replicate the commercial success of So Tonight That I Might See but is often cited by fans as the band's most purely atmospheric record.
Mazzy Star.lineage: Closes out Mazzy Star's classic run on its most downbeat note, an influence on the drawled, reverb-soaked side of both sadcore and the later Hope Sandoval solo work.

Meat Puppets.description: The Kirkwood brothers and Derrick Bostrom's debut is blistering, blown-out hardcore, recorded fast and cheap, that gives almost no hint of the psychedelic country turn the band would take one album later. Curt Kirkwood's guitar is pure noise here, and the songs blur together at hardcore speed with little of the melody that would define Meat Puppets II. It is mostly valuable now as the extreme starting point of one of SST's strangest, most unpredictable trajectories.
Meat Puppets.lineage: The Phoenix trio's hardcore-only SST debut, made before their sudden and total swerve into cowpunk psychedelia on Meat Puppets II a year later.

Meat Puppets.description: One of the most startling stylistic pivots in SST's catalog: a hardcore band suddenly playing loose, desert-baked country-psych, with Curt Kirkwood's cracked, off-key voice and rambling guitar lines sounding like Crazy Horse filtered through acid and punk indifference to polish. 'Plateau,' 'Oh, Me,' and 'Lake of Fire' would later become famous through Nirvana's MTV Unplugged covers, but here they are rawer and stranger, closer to a campfire séance than a rock record. It effectively invented a whole strand of cowpunk-gone-cosmic that echoes through alt-country decades later.
Meat Puppets.lineage: A radical, hardcore-to-cosmic-country swerve that directly influenced Nirvana (who covered three songs from it on MTV Unplugged) and prefigured the psychedelic, Crazy-Horse-indebted wing of alt-country and slacker rock.

Meat Puppets.description: Brighter and jazzier than the murky Meat Puppets II, built on clean, interlocking guitar lines that ripple and shimmer rather than crash, closer to a desert-rock take on Television than to punk. Curt Kirkwood's voice is still ragged but the songs float rather than lurch, an almost weightless take on jam-band psychedelia filtered through SST's DIY economy. It is arguably the most purely beautiful record to come out of the SST roster.
Meat Puppets.lineage: The middle panel of the Meat Puppets' mid-80s trilogy, moving even further from hardcore into a clean, interwoven-guitar psychedelia that anticipated jangly desert and cosmic-country indie bands decades later.

Meat Puppets.description: A denser, more heavily arranged continuation of Up on the Sun's desert psychedelia, with the Kirkwoods layering more overdubs and studio effects than on any previous record. It trades some of the earlier records' raw immediacy for a more deliberate, atmospheric feel, closer to a Southwestern hallucination than a live band jamming in a room. Fans of the trilogy's earlier records tend to call it underrated, overshadowed by its more iconic siblings.
Meat Puppets.lineage: The third record in the Meat Puppets' mid-80s cosmic-country run, made as the band's SST tenure was winding toward its more rock-oriented late-80s phase.

Meat Puppets.description: A deliberate lurch toward straightforward, boogie-rock guitar heroics, heavier and more macho than anything else in the Meat Puppets catalog, with Curt Kirkwood indulging in long, unapologetic guitar solos over a more conventional rock backbeat. It sacrifices some of the earlier records' strangeness for pure riff-driven momentum, a record the band has described as intentionally dumb fun. It remains divisive among longtime fans precisely because it is the least 'cosmic' of the trilogy-plus records.
Meat Puppets.lineage: A conscious pivot toward Crazy-Horse-style riff rock, released the same year as Mirage; it shows the Meat Puppets testing how far their SST audience would follow them toward straight rock before the Monsters and major-label years.

Meat Puppets.description: The Meat Puppets' last SST album pushes further into arena-scaled classic rock, with cleaner production and longer, more conventionally structured songs than anything since the hardcore debut. It closes out the band's independent-label run on a note that clearly aims at the major-label rock audience they would find with the London Records deal that followed. Longtime fans of the weirder mid-80s records tend to see it as the sound of the band outgrowing SST.
Meat Puppets.lineage: The final Meat Puppets album on SST before the band's early-90s major-label period, closing out one of the label's strangest and most musically varied catalogs.

Meernaa.description: Three-song EP of slow-motion, synth-tinged dream-folk from Carly Bond's San Francisco project: sparse arrangements, cavernous reverb and a fragile, close-mic'd vocal at the center.
Meernaa.lineage: Extends Meernaa's hushed, slowcore-adjacent songwriting between Duster-style haze and modern indie folk.

Meg Baird.description: Recorded while Baird was still a member of Philadelphia psych-folk band Espers, her solo debut is a hushed, largely solo-voice-and-guitar record of traditional and original ballads, her clear, unadorned alto compared by critics to Sandy Denny and Pentangle's Jacqui McShee. It is one of the plainest, most old-time-adjacent records to come out of the 2000s Philadelphia freak-folk scene. A quiet, patient entry point for listeners who want folk-revival singing without ornamentation.
Meg Baird.lineage: Grew out of Baird's time in Espers and the Philadelphia psych-folk scene, carrying Anglo-American folk-ballad singing into the indie-folk revival alongside Gillian Welch and Iron & Wine.

Mega Bog.description: Erin Birgy's surrealist song-world turns painterly and desert-lit on this record, co-produced with Big Thief's James Krivchenia: avant-pop arrangements wrapped around plainspoken, image-dense lyrics.
Mega Bog.lineage: Connected to the Big Thief/indie-folk network via Krivchenia's production; sits at the arty edge of the twangy indie-folk lane.

Megafaun.description: Formed by two former members of DeYarmond Edison (the band Justin Vernon left to start Bon Iver), Megafaun's second album blends front-porch folk, gospel harmony and loose improvisation into a warm, communal record. It established the Durham-based trio as a key node of the Triangle's freak-folk-adjacent scene.
Megafaun.lineage: Grew out of the breakup of DeYarmond Edison, carrying that band's Wisconsin-to-North Carolina folk experimentation into a looser, more communal direction.

Megafaun.description: A shorter release between the band's two full-lengths, continuing the warm, harmony-driven folk of 'Gather, Form & Fly' in a more compact set of songs. It shows the trio refining rather than reinventing its communal, gospel-inflected sound.
Megafaun.lineage: A bridge between 'Gather, Form & Fly' and the band's self-titled 2011 album, keeping the same warm vocal-harmony approach.

Melissa Carper.description: A double-bassist steeped in old-time, blues, and Western swing, Carper's Rolling Stone-lauded second solo album mixes vintage upright-bass swing with plainspoken country songwriting delivered in a warm, unhurried voice. It sounds like a lost 1950s record more than a contemporary one. A quiet standout of the classicist wing of the scene.
Melissa Carper.lineage: Draws on Western swing and old-time double-bass traditions, connecting the neo-outlaw revival to pre-war and honky-tonk-era country bass playing.

Merce Lemon.album: Watch Me Drive Them Dogs Wild
Merce Lemon.description: Pittsburgh songwriter's breakout LP: warbling steel and outlaw-tinged guitars swelling into feedback-heavy catharsis, produced by Colin Miller and Alex Farrar at Drop of Sun; songs of loss, land and family community.
Merce Lemon.lineage: Ties Merce Lemon into the Asheville production network (Colin Miller, Alex Farrar, Xandy Chelmis of Wednesday on pedal steel) shared with Florry and Wednesday.

Merle Haggard.description: A world-weary late-1970s record built around drinking and touring-life songs, written mostly by Haggard himself as his personal life and marriages were unraveling. The band sounds a little rougher and more road-worn than the Capitol-era Strangers records, matching lyrics about hangovers, motel rooms, and burned-out relationships. It is often cited as one of his most autobiographical and least commercial-minded 1970s albums.
Merle Haggard.lineage: A late, harder-bitten entry in Haggard's honky-tonk lineage that connects his 1960s persona to the more confessional, worn-in songwriting of 1980s country and the outlaw scene's back half.

Merle Haggard.description: Recorded with fiddler-guitarist Leona Williams and longtime picker Roy Nichols, the title track's plea to trade city life for a green California county became one of Haggard's signature later hits. It is a straightforward, unfussy honky-tonk record, closer in spirit to his 1960s Capitol albums than to the more polished country of the early 1980s around it. It shows the Bakersfield sound still commercially viable a decade and a half after Strangers.
Merle Haggard.lineage: A late-career return to the plain, Telecaster-driven Bakersfield sound of Haggard's Capitol years, made just as neo-traditionalists like George Strait were about to make that plainness fashionable again.

Merle Haggard and the Strangers.description: Merle Haggard's debut LP lays out the stripped-down Bakersfield sound he built with his band the Strangers: a stinging Telecaster and pedal steel trading lines over a tight rhythm section, with none of the string sections softening Nashville records of the same year. The title track and "(My Friends Are Gonna Be) Strangers" set up the plainspoken, first-person voice of hard living and loneliness that would define his whole catalog. It is the sound of a singer still finding his footing but already sure of his instrumentation.
Merle Haggard and the Strangers.lineage: Extends the Bakersfield honky-tonk sound Buck Owens and Wynn Stewart had already popularized, and opens the run of Haggard albums through the 1970s that became the hard-country reference point.

Merle Haggard and the Strangers.album: Swinging Doors and the Bottle Let Me Down
Merle Haggard and the Strangers.description: Two of Haggard's signature honky-tonk singles, "Swinging Doors" and "The Bottle Let Me Down," anchor this album, both sung with the matter-of-fact ache that separated him from novelty drinking songs. James Burton and Roy Nichols-style Telecaret leads (played here by the Strangers) keep the arrangements lean and barroom-ready rather than orchestral. It topped the country album chart and set the template of tight, unglamorous production Haggard kept for the rest of the decade.
Merle Haggard and the Strangers.lineage: Follows directly from Strangers and cements the Haggard/Strangers honky-tonk sound that Bakersfield acts like Gary Stewart and later alt-country bands kept citing.

Merle Haggard and the Strangers.description: Built around the title hit, this album pushed Haggard's outlaw-on-the-run persona to the front, drawing loosely on his own years in San Quentin. The Strangers keep the sound spare and rhythmic, built for dancehalls rather than string sections, with Haggard's voice sitting low and conversational in the mix. It is one of the records that made his biography inseparable from his songwriting.
Merle Haggard and the Strangers.lineage: Deepens the ex-con storytelling voice introduced on Strangers and points toward the more explicitly autobiographical Sing Me Back Home and Mama Tried the following year.

Merle Haggard and the Strangers.description: Haggard confronts his prison record head-on in the title track, one of country music's first hit singles to openly discuss a criminal past, and the rest of the LP follows suit with unsentimental songs about second chances and small-town judgment. The Strangers' playing stays tight and unadorned, letting Haggard's flat, weathered baritone carry the weight. It is a key document of the Bakersfield sound treating hard biography as legitimate subject matter rather than novelty.
Merle Haggard and the Strangers.lineage: Continues the ex-convict narrative voice from I'm a Lonesome Fugitive and hardens the template later outlaw-country writers like Waylon Jennings and David Allan Coe drew on.

Merle Haggard and the Strangers.description: The title track, a death-row ballad reportedly inspired by an execution Haggard witnessed in San Quentin, is among the bleakest and most quietly devastating songs of his career, sung without melodrama over a simple waltz-time arrangement. The rest of the record mixes similarly plainspoken narratives with a couple of gospel-tinged numbers, keeping the Strangers' backing lean throughout. It shows Haggard using the Bakersfield sound's plainness as a tool for genuine pathos rather than barroom rowdiness.
Merle Haggard and the Strangers.lineage: Sits between Branded Man and Mama Tried in Haggard's run of ex-convict narratives, and its restraint influenced later story-songwriters from the outlaw scene through Steve Earle.

Merle Haggard and the Strangers.description: The title song is Haggard's most concise statement of the outlaw-son narrative that ran through his early work, a two-minute confession of a mother's failed efforts set to a driving Bakersfield shuffle. Roy Nichols's Telecaster lines and the Strangers' unfussy backing keep the record moving at a dancehall pace even on its sadder numbers. It remains the most commonly cited entry point into Haggard's catalog and into the whole Bakersfield sound.
Merle Haggard and the Strangers.lineage: The culmination of Haggard's 1967-68 run of ex-convict songs, and a direct touchstone for everyone from the Grateful Dead (who covered the title track) to 1990s alt-country bands.

Merle Haggard and the Strangers.description: Recorded as Haggard's persona shifted from outlaw to working-class spokesman, this album mixes barroom shuffles with more overtly patriotic and blue-collar material, previewing the direction "Okie from Muskogee" would take later that year. The Strangers keep the arrangements built around Telecaster and fiddle, still recognizably Bakersfield rather than Nashville-polished. It is a transitional record between the prison-song era and Haggard's turn as country music's voice of the silent majority.
Merle Haggard and the Strangers.lineage: Bridges the ex-convict narratives of Branded Man and Sing Me Back Home with the working-class populism of Okie from Muskogee and the records that followed it.

Merle Haggard and the Strangers.description: A full double-LP tribute to Jimmie Rodgers, recut with the Strangers rather than covered note-for-note, this record makes explicit the direct line from 1920s blue-yodel country to Bakersfield honky-tonk. Haggard's plain baritone stands in for Rodgers's yodel, and the arrangements lean on train-song rhythm and harmonica rather than reproducing period instrumentation exactly. It is as much a statement of lineage as it is a tribute record, tying the whole Bakersfield project back to hillbilly music's founding figure.
Merle Haggard and the Strangers.lineage: Explicitly connects Haggard's Bakersfield sound back to Jimmie Rodgers and the pre-1965 country roots this lane's parent lane (Roots) covers.

Merle Haggard and the Strangers.description: Recorded live in Muskogee, Oklahoma, this album turns the title single (a wry, deliberately square rebuttal to late-1960s counterculture) into a full concert statement, with the crowd audibly cheering the song's small-town pride. The band plays it loose and rowdy compared to the studio records, closer to a real dancehall set than a polished live album. It became one of the most political and most quoted country records of its era, embraced and parodied in roughly equal measure.
Merle Haggard and the Strangers.lineage: Grows out of Pride in What I Am's working-class themes and turns Haggard into the era's most visible country voice on the other side of the culture wars from Woodstock-adjacent rock.

Merle Haggard and the Strangers.description: A quieter, more reflective record than the outlaw-narrative albums of the late 1960s, Hag leans into ballads and mid-tempo numbers with the Strangers playing in a more understated, jazz-inflected mode led by Haggard's own fiddle and guitar interests. It shows the range underneath the honky-tonk persona, closer to a singer-songwriter record than a barroom set. Critics at the time noted it as one of his more personal, less single-driven albums.
Merle Haggard and the Strangers.lineage: Part of Haggard's early-1970s turn toward more varied, album-oriented work between the topical hits of Okie from Muskogee and the song-based records that followed.

Merle Haggard and the Strangers.description: A loose, warm album named for its title track's picture of hard times endured together, this record leans toward mid-tempo country-soul phrasing rather than the harder Bakersfield shuffle of Haggard's late-1960s work. The Strangers' playing is relaxed and confident, and Haggard's writing turns toward gratitude and perspective rather than outlaw drama. It is a good example of how quickly Haggard's songwriting matured past novelty and persona.
Merle Haggard and the Strangers.lineage: Represents the more reflective, adult-pop-leaning side of Haggard's early-1970s catalog, a strand that later informed the songwriterly wing of outlaw country.

Merle Haggard and the Strangers.album: Let Me Tell You About a Song
Merle Haggard and the Strangers.description: An unusual concept record in which Haggard introduces several songs with spoken narration explaining their origins, turning the album into part performance, part oral history of his own catalog and influences. The device foregrounds the storytelling instinct that runs under all of his honky-tonk records, and the songs themselves range from newly written material to older favorites re-cut with the Strangers. It is a deep cut but a revealing one about how deliberately Haggard built his persona.
Merle Haggard and the Strangers.lineage: An unusually explicit statement of the storytelling ethic that runs through the whole Bakersfield/hard-country lane, later echoed by songwriter-focused liner-note and spoken-intro records elsewhere in country and Americana.

Merle Haggard and the Strangers.album: If We Make It Through December
Merle Haggard and the Strangers.description: The title track, a spare Christmas-season song about a laid-off factory worker unable to provide for his family, became one of Haggard's biggest hits and one of country music's bleakest holiday songs, delivered with none of the genre's usual seasonal cheer. The rest of the album keeps to similarly plainspoken, working-class material rather than filler novelty songs. It stands as one of the clearest statements of Haggard's blue-collar realism.
Merle Haggard and the Strangers.lineage: Continues the working-class storytelling of Pride in What I Am and Okie from Muskogee, and its unsentimental view of hard times influenced later Southern storytellers like the Drive-By Truckers.

Mess Esque.description: Mess Esque's third album is a twisted, handmade folk record from Helen Franzmann (McKisko) and Mick Turner (Dirty Three), eight songs that build a warm, dreamlike world out of plainspoken vocals and loose, unhurried arrangements. It sounds openhearted and slightly askew at once.
Mess Esque.lineage: Released on Drag City, placing Mess Esque squarely within that label's deadpan, wry songwriting lineage alongside Bill Callahan and Bonnie 'Prince' Billy.

Michael Chapman.description: Chapman's second album, cut with a pre-fame Mick Ronson on lead guitar and Rick Kemp (soon of Steeleye Span) on bass, is built around his best-known song, 'Postcards of Scarborough,' a plainspoken portrait of a fading English seaside town. His guitar playing draws on the same fingerstyle vocabulary as Bert Jansch and Davy Graham, but his gravelly, conversational voice and travelogue lyrics push the songs closer to folk-rock storytelling than pure guitar showcase. John Peel championed the record on his radio show, helping it reach UK No. 45.
Michael Chapman.lineage: Shares session players and a Yorkshire folk-club background with Steeleye Span and the wider Transatlantic/Harvest folk scene, and Chapman's plainspoken storytelling and open-tuned guitar work influenced later British guitarists like Jack Rose's American Primitive circle.

Michael Chapman.description: Marking fifty years since his first record, Chapman's Paradise of Bachelors debut pairs his weathered English fingerstyle guitar with a hushed, world-weary voice and guest guitar from Steve Gunn, mixing acoustic and electric arrangements into a late-career highlight. It is not an instrumental record, but Chapman's guitar playing, direct and unshowy, has long been claimed by American Primitive listeners and labels as a British parallel to Fahey's generation. The record introduced Chapman to a new American underground audience decades into his career.
Michael Chapman.lineage: A British contemporary of the original American Primitive generation whose intricate steel-string playing has long been championed by that scene's labels and younger players like Steve Gunn, even though most of his records, this one included, are built around his own singing.

Michael Chapman.description: Chapman's debut LP is psychedelic-tinged British folk-guitar songwriting, produced by Gus Dudgeon, with his weathered baritone over fingerpicked and occasionally full-band arrangements. It opens with his best-known song, "It Didn't Work Out," and moves through wistful, understated ballads. A key entry point into the British folk-rock guitar tradition that indie folk and American Primitive players still cite.
Michael Chapman.lineage: Part of the same late-60s UK folk-guitar wave as Bert Jansch and Nick Drake; Chapman's fingerstyle playing directly influenced American Primitive guitarists and later indie-folk songwriters.

Michael Hurley.description: A wandering old-time songwriter whose loose, talky phrasing and dry, cracked-voice humor decades later made him a patron saint of the Drag City deadpan school, Hurley's early Raccoon Records albums mix hand-drawn cover art, werewolf mythology and plainspoken country-blues into a sound that is equal parts front-porch and cosmic joke. Armchair Boogie is looser and warmer than his later Drag City-era records but already has the wry, unhurried delivery that Will Oldham and Bill Callahan would later cite as an influence. Predates the lane's 1990-2026 window but is logged here as the deadpan patriarch.
Michael Hurley.lineage: A direct ancestor of the Drag City deadpan style; Hurley later released records on Gnomonsong and was championed by the Drag City circle, making his early-1970s catalog a documented root of the sound even though it predates the lane's era.

Michael Hurley.description: The follow-up to Armchair Boogie continues Hurley's homemade, talking-blues style, recorded with the same loose, unhurried feel and dry sense of humor about small-town life and animal folklore. His plain, weathered voice and refusal to polish anything became a touchstone for the generation of Drag City songwriters who discovered him decades later. A key record for understanding where the label's deadpan aesthetic ultimately traces back to.
Michael Hurley.lineage: Continues directly from Armchair Boogie in the same Raccoon Records run; Hurley's whole catalog is a documented influence on Will Oldham and the Drag City roster, who helped bring him to a new generation of listeners in the 2000s.

Michael Hurley.description: The outsider-folk elder's early-2000s album keeps his loose, homemade blend of country blues, folk and talking-blues humor, sung in his cracked, conversational drawl. Arrangements stay sparse and unhurried, prioritizing songs and character sketches over polish. A representative later-period entry in a catalog that quietly shaped the Drag City/Palace generation's plainspoken songwriting.
Michael Hurley.lineage: A key link between the 1960s Greenwich Village folk scene (he recorded for Folkways as a teenager) and the Drag City circle, who idolized him and released his later records; his loose, funny-sad style directly informed Will Oldham and Silver Jews.

Michael Hurley.description: Recorded with the indie-folk band Ida, this Gnomonsong release (the label run by Vetiver's Andy Cabic and Devendra Banhart) frames Hurley's rambling country-blues songs in gentle full-band arrangements. His cracked, easygoing voice stays the center, but the backing is warmer and fuller than his solo records. A good look at how the 2000s freak-folk generation embraced him as an elder statesman.
Michael Hurley.lineage: Part of the 2000s freak-folk/New Weird America rediscovery of Hurley by artists like Vetiver and Devendra Banhart; extends his direct influence on the Drag City deadpan-folk lineage into a new generation.

Michael Hurley & Ida.description: A full collaboration between Hurley and the hushed Brooklyn folk trio Ida, released on the Gnomonsong label Devendra Banhart and Vetiver's Andy Cabic ran to champion older folk eccentrics, this pairs Hurley's wandering drawl with Ida's close, quiet harmonies. It softens his usual talking-blues looseness into something gentler and more arranged than his solo records. A good way into Hurley's later-period work for listeners coming from indie folk rather than old-time music.
Michael Hurley & Ida.lineage: A documented link between Hurley's decades-old deadpan-folk style and the 2000s indie-folk revival, both through Ida's own hushed harmony sound and Gnomonsong's role in reintroducing him to a younger audience.

Michael Hurley, the Unholy Modal Rounder.description: A shared-vocal collaborative album between Michael Hurley, Peter Stampfel's Unholy Modal Rounders and Jeffrey Frederick's Clamtones, Have Moicy! is a loose, funny, deceptively wise record of talking-blues and old-time-shaped songs that critic Robert Christgau named his favorite album of its year. Its blend of jokes, folklore and plain-voiced sincerity anticipated the exact tone the Drag City deadpan school would later prize in Silver Jews and Palace. Essential listening for tracing the deadpan-funny-sad lineage back to its 1970s roots.
Michael Hurley, the Unholy Modal Rounder.lineage: A landmark collaboration between Michael Hurley and the Holy Modal Rounders circle, both explicitly credited by the assignment as ancestors of the Drag City deadpan school; the record's mix of humor and plainspoken sadness is a direct, documented root of the trunk line running from Prine through Drag City to today.

Michael Martin Murphey.description: Michael Martin Murphey's debut, produced by Bob Johnston in Nashville, mixes protest songwriting (the title track's sympathy for Geronimo) with the loose, string-band feel that became known as 'cosmic cowboy' music back in Austin. 'Backslider's Wine' would later become a Viva Terlingua highlight in Jerry Jeff Walker's hands, showing how tightly the Austin songwriters traded material. Rolling Stone singled him out early as one of the best new songwriters in the country, and the record helped put Austin's emerging scene on the national map.
Michael Martin Murphey.lineage: Coined and popularized the 'cosmic cowboy' tag for the Austin progressive-country scene, directly feeding the same circle that produced Jerry Jeff Walker's Viva Terlingua and B.W. Stevenson's records.

Michael Martin Murphey.description: Murphey's second album names the Austin scene outright with 'Cosmic Cowboy, Pt. 1' and 'Alleys of Austin,' turning the loose, country-rock-meets-folk sound of his debut into a genre statement. The songs stretch out more than typical AM radio country, with 'South Canadian River Song' running past seven minutes on gentle, unhurried instrumental passages. It is the record most responsible for putting a name on the whole hippie-country movement gathering around the Armadillo World Headquarters in Austin.
Michael Martin Murphey.lineage: Gave the 'cosmic cowboy' scene its name, directly describing the same Austin crowd (Jerry Jeff Walker, Willie Nelson, Rusty Wier) that the rest of this lane's Austin artists belonged to.

Michael Nesmith.album: And the Hits Just Keep On Comin'
Michael Nesmith.description: A stripped-back, mostly acoustic duo record with just Nesmith and virtuoso guitarist Red Rhodes (on both steel and acoustic), re-recording some earlier songs alongside new ones in a spare, intimate setting. It is one of Nesmith's most purely country records, closer to a demo session than a produced album, and it shows how central Rhodes' playing was to his whole sound. It was released solo, without a full backing band credit.
Michael Nesmith.lineage: A stripped-down, acoustic-leaning Michael Nesmith record built entirely around his long partnership with steel guitarist Red Rhodes.

Michael Nesmith & the First National Ban.description: Fresh out of the Monkees, Nesmith formed the First National Band around pedal steel player Red Rhodes and cut a record of loose, warm country rock built on his own wry, plainspoken songwriting. Joanne became his biggest solo hit, but the whole album has the same unhurried, Bakersfield-tinged feel. It is often overlooked next to the Byrds/Burritos axis but was recorded and released right alongside them.
Michael Nesmith & the First National Ban.lineage: Michael Nesmith's first post-Monkees country-rock album, built around steel guitarist Red Rhodes' playing, which became as identifiable a voice in this lane as Sneaky Pete's.

Michael Nesmith & the First National Ban.description: The second First National Band record, released the same year as Magnetic South, keeps the same Red Rhodes-driven sound and adds a hit-charting cover of Different Drum, the song Nesmith wrote that made Linda Ronstadt's Stone Poneys famous. It is a slightly more relaxed, road-worn record than the debut. Commercially it did less well despite the built-in hook of that song's history.
Michael Nesmith & the First National Ban.lineage: Continues the First National Band's country-rock sound from Magnetic South within the same year.

Michael Nesmith & the First National Ban.description: The First National Band's third and final album mixes originals with outside songwriters and leans a touch more pop than the first two, recorded as the band was already starting to dissolve. It closes out Nesmith's most straightforwardly country-rock period before he moved toward looser, odder solo records with the Second National Band. Red Rhodes' steel is still the record's signature texture.
Michael Nesmith & the First National Ban.lineage: The last First National Band record, closing that chapter before Nesmith's more eclectic Second National Band and solo work.

Michelle Shocked.description: Recorded partly live at the Kerrville Folk Festival on a cheap cassette deck and partly in a London studio, Short Sharp Shocked mixes folk protest songwriting with a punk-scene toughness Shocked picked up from the San Francisco squatter and activist circuit. Anchorage became a surprise college-radio hit, and the albums plainspoken political songs made her an unlikely folk star at the height of the Reagan era. It is a foundational record for the folk-punk crossover that fed directly into 1990s alt-country and Americana.
Michelle Shocked.lineage: Came out of the same cowpunk and folk-punk crossover scene as X and the Blasters, and its blend of acoustic folk songwriting with a punk sensibility anticipated the alt-country movement that broke a few years later.

Mickey Newbury.description: Mickey Newbury's second album is a moody concept record stitched together with recurring rain sound effects, turning a suite of heartbreak songs into something closer to a spoken-word tone poem than a conventional country record. 'She Even Woke Me Up to Say Goodbye' and an early version of 'San Francisco Mabel Joy' show Newbury's hushed baritone and unhurried, almost cinematic phrasing. It became a quiet touchstone for the outlaw country songwriters who followed him in Nashville.
Mickey Newbury.lineage: Newbury's Nashville circle overlapped directly with Kris Kristofferson and Waylon Jennings, feeding the outlaw country movement he helped inspire, while his mood-piece song construction anticipated the concept-album approach Lee Hazlewood was building on the West Coast at the same time.

Mickey Newbury.description: 'Frisco Mabel Joy is Newbury's best-known album, built around 'An American Trilogy,' his medley of two Civil War-era songs and a spiritual that Elvis Presley later turned into a Las Vegas showstopper. The rest of the record keeps the same hushed, orchestrated melancholy, with 'How I Love Them Old Songs' and 'The Future's Not What It Used to Be' showing Newbury's gift for wistful, plainly sung reflection. It remains the most widely covered entry in his catalog.
Mickey Newbury.lineage: Written within the same early-1970s Nashville songwriter circle as Kris Kristofferson and Tom T. Hall, and its orchestral, mood-first production directly influenced the countrypolitan wing of 1970s Nashville songwriting.

Mickey Newbury.description: Heaven Help the Child continues Newbury's run of hushed, orchestrated song cycles, built around the wrenching multi-generational title track and 'Cortelia Clark,' a haunting tribute to a blind street singer who died in a house fire. 'Why You Been Gone So Long' became one of Newbury's most recorded compositions in bluegrass circles, showing how his songs traveled even when his own recordings stayed under the radar. The record extends the tone-poem approach of Looks Like Rain into even bleaker territory.
Mickey Newbury.lineage: Completes a run of early-1970s mood-piece albums that made Newbury one of Nashville's most respected songwriters' songwriters, a reputation that fed directly into the outlaw country movement around him.

Mikaela Davis.description: Davis's classically-trained harp anchors a full-band record made with longtime collaborators, weaving 60s pop melodies, psychedelia and driving folk rock. Fans compare it to Fleetwood Mac at their most collaborative; steel guitarist Kurt Johnson gives it a country-rock backbone.
Mikaela Davis.lineage: Davis has shared stages with Bob Weir, Phil Lesh and Circles Around the Sun, and this record leans into that Dead-adjacent, harmony-driven jam-pop lineage.

Mikaela Davis.description: A 'canyon country' record written in a Chevy Chase Canyon hillside home, tying a neo-western future to Laurel Canyon's lineage and the mythos of Elvis's Graceland. It balances light and dark more explicitly than her earlier records while keeping her harp and full-band folk-rock sound intact.
Mikaela Davis.lineage: Continues Davis's arc from harp-led chamber pop toward explicit Laurel Canyon/cosmic-country songwriting.

Mike Cooley.description: A solo acoustic live album recorded in Atlanta, stripping Drive-By Truckers songs like 'Zip City' and 'Marry Me' down to just Cooley's voice, guitar and dry between-song banter. It highlights Cooley's plainer, funnier, more deadpan songwriting style, since there is no full band arrangement to fill in the space. As his only official solo release, it is a rare chance to hear the other half of DBT's two-songwriter partnership on his own.
Mike Cooley.lineage: A solo live document from the guitarist and co-songwriter who, with Patterson Hood, has anchored Drive-By Truckers since its 1996 formation in Athens, Georgia.

Mildred.description: The Oakland quartet's breezy, affecting debut LP built from four singers and songwriters trading lead vocals, ranging from laconic to full-throated. Conversational lyrics and a living-room-session intimacy carry the funny-sad, plainspoken storytelling that puts them in the same lineage as their labelmates.
Mildred.lineage: Debut full-length following the mild EP; part of the Memorials of Distinction/Dog Day Records roster alongside Brad Goodall.

Mildred.description: Mildred's four-song debut EP, recorded over a couple of weekends in a shared living room with janky microphones, introduces the four-singer, four-songwriter format they'd expand on Fenceline.
Mildred.lineage: Precedes Fenceline; the band's origin document as former roommates turned bandmates.

Mineral.description: A Texas emo landmark of quiet-loud dynamics and raw, cracked-voice catharsis, considered alongside Diary as a genre-defining second-wave emo record despite the band's short lifespan.
Mineral.lineage: Sits alongside Sunny Day Real Estate in the second-wave emo line growing out of V16's underground rock scene, feeding the 2000s emo mainstream rather than the Core.

Minor Moon.description: Sam Cantor's Chicago band mixes alt-country songwriting with adventurous, Dead-like guitar theatrics and Max Subar's pedal steel, backed by a rotating cast of Chicago players including Sima Cunningham and Macie Stewart. Josh Terry, who wrote the album's bio, called it his favorite Chicago band's best work.
Minor Moon.lineage: Part of the same Chicago DIY web as Liam Kazar and Spencer Radcliffe, drawing on Grateful Dead and Crazy Horse guitar lineage filtered through Midwestern alt-country songwriting.

Minor Moon.description: Recorded at Chicago's Thawed Out festival in 2025, this live document catches Sam Cantor's band stretching their warm, Dead-adjacent country-rock songs out on stage. Terry has named Minor Moon among his favorite Chicago bands.
Minor Moon.lineage: A live snapshot of Chicago's own small cosmic-country scene, adjacent to acts like Ryley Walker in the city's guitar-forward underground.

Minor Threat.description: Since Minor Threat never released a studio LP, this Dischord compilation collecting the band's two early-80s EPs (including the Minor Threat and Out of Step sessions) is the canonical way to hear Ian MacKaye's foundational straight-edge hardcore. Tight, fast and moralistic, it defined both the musical and ethical template (DIY labels, no drugs, no sellouts) that the whole American hardcore underground inherited. Essential for the DIY-network trunk line this lane sits under.
Minor Threat.lineage: Descends from the same New York/DC hardcore acceleration of punk (alongside Bad Brains and Black Flag) that this lane covers; feeds directly into Dischord's DIY-label model and the American underground/college rock scene (V16) rather than back toward earlier UK or NY punk.

Minutemen.description: Eighteen songs in fifteen minutes, none of them sounding quite like hardcore even though the tempos are just as fast: D. Boon's clanging, almost jazz-inflected guitar and Mike Watt's rubbery bass turn punk speed into something closer to agit-funk collage. Lyrics are terse, political, and often funny, delivered in Boon's untrained bellow with none of the macho posturing common to the scene around them. It set the template of extreme economy and genre-scrambling the band would expand on for the rest of the decade.
Minutemen.lineage: The San Pedro trio's SST debut, made as founding labelmates alongside Black Flag; its funk-and-jazz-inflected attack on hardcore orthodoxy became a direct influence on fIREHOSE, the Meat Puppets' loose SST peers, and later post-hardcore bands like Fugazi.

Minutemen.album: What Makes a Man Start Fires?
Minutemen.description: Denser and more abrasive than the debut, with George Hurley's drumming pushed forward and D. Boon's guitar leaning into dissonance and start-stop rhythms that owe as much to Captain Beefheart as to punk. The songs remain compact and politically pointed, but the arrangements are more adventurous, hinting at the sprawl of Double Nickels a year later. It is the least accessible Minutemen record but arguably the most purely experimental.
Minutemen.lineage: The trio's second SST full-length, tightening the political, funk-punk collage approach of The Punch Line into something stranger, right before it exploded outward on Double Nickels on the Dime.

Minutemen.album: Buzz or Howl Under the Influence of Heat
Minutemen.description: A tight seven-song EP that pushes further into the loose, dubby, almost funk-jazz territory the band had been circling, with Watt's bass often carrying the melody while Boon's guitar scratches and jabs around it. It is looser and warmer than What Makes a Man Start Fires?, closer in spirit to the more playful moments of Double Nickels on the Dime that would follow it within a year. Even at its most exploratory, the band keeps the songs under two minutes.
Minutemen.lineage: A quick SST EP bridging the more abrasive What Makes a Man Start Fires? and the band's genre-scrambling commercial and critical peak, Double Nickels on the Dime.

Minutemen.description: A forty-five-song double album recorded partly as a good-natured response to Hüsker Dü's Zen Arcade, careening through punk, funk, spoken word, and country-tinged interludes without ever settling into one genre for long. D. Boon and Mike Watt trade blue-collar, working-class lyrics with real political bite, delivered over some of the most rhythmically inventive punk-adjacent music of the decade. It is widely regarded as the Minutemen's masterpiece and one of the defining SST records of the 1980s.
Minutemen.lineage: Recorded as a direct answer to Hüsker Dü's double-LP ambitions; its genre-scrambling, working-class songwriting made it the most influential SST record after Zen Arcade and a touchstone for the Meat Puppets, fIREHOSE, and later post-hardcore and indie bands alike.

Minutemen.description: The band's final studio album before D. Boon's death in a December 1985 van accident, released just weeks before he died, still restless and eclectic, closing with a faithful cover of Steppenwolf's 'Born to Be Wild' that reframes the biker anthem as blue-collar irony. It is a slightly more relaxed, groove-oriented record than Double Nickels, but no less politically engaged or genre-agnostic. Its release under tragic circumstances turned it into an unintended farewell.
Minutemen.lineage: The Minutemen's last album, released just before D. Boon's death ended the band; Mike Watt and George Hurley would carry the group's loose, funk-inflected SST sound forward into fIREHOSE within a year.

Miracle Legion.description: Mark Mulcahy's Connecticut band builds a ringing, R.E.M.-adjacent jangle around his distinctive, quavering voice, closer in spirit to Southern gothic storytelling than to the punk energy of the SST-scene bands around them. The bonus-track cover of Mission of Burma's 'Academy Fight Song' underlines how tightly the mid-80s American underground's regional scenes overlapped despite their different sounds. It is a quietly literate, melancholy record that earned comparisons to R.E.M. throughout its initial reviews.
Miracle Legion.lineage: A Connecticut jangle-pop band frequently compared to R.E.M. in the mid-80s music press, extending the Southern-inflected jangle sound into New England's college-radio scene.

Mission of Burma.description: Mission of Burma's only studio album from their original run pairs blaring, tape-loop-treated guitar squall with tightly wound rhythms and Roger Miller and Clint Conley's alternating shouted vocals. It became a foundational text for American noise-rock and post-hardcore despite selling few copies at the time. Essential for the angular, rhythmic line that runs from Boston's scene through Fugazi and beyond.
Mission of Burma.lineage: An American, Boston-scene branch off X14's punk foundation and V29's art-noise lineage; its tape-loop noise and structural aggression directly informed Sonic Youth, Hüsker Dü and the noise-rock wing of X10 rather than any twang-adjacent lane.

Mission of Burma.description: Reuniting after a 20-year hiatus, Mission of Burma sound barely diminished on ONoffON, matching Vs.'s aggression with slightly cleaner production and Bob Weston (of Shellac) replacing original tape-loop manipulator Martin Swope. It proved the band's reunion was substance over nostalgia. A useful modern example of the lane's founders still working.
Mission of Burma.lineage: A late-career continuation of Mission of Burma's original branch off X14/V29's noise-punk lineage, with a Shellac/Big Black connection tying it to the Chicago noise-rock wing of the same lane.

Mississippi John Hurt.album: Avalon Blues: The Complete 1928 Okeh Recordings
Mississippi John Hurt.description: Hurt's two 1928 OKeh sessions produced a gentle, syncopated fingerpicking style and a warm, unhurried singing voice utterly unlike the harder Delta blues of his contemporaries, on songs like 'Frankie' and 'Candy Man Blues.' The records sold poorly and Hurt returned to farming in Avalon, Mississippi for over three decades until a blues researcher traced him there in 1963 using clues from one of these very songs. This Columbia/Legacy set gathers the complete, foundational sessions that made his later rediscovery possible.
Mississippi John Hurt.lineage: His gentle fingerstyle approach became a direct model for the American Primitive guitarists (John Fahey specifically cited him) and for 1960s folk-revival guitarists like Doc Watson and Dave Van Ronk.

Mitski.album: The Land Is Inhospitable and So Are We
Mitski.description: Mitski strips back her usual maximalism for a hushed, string-laden record that Wikipedia describes as Americana, country and folk-inflected, closer to spare orchestral pop than any Nashville sound. Josh Terry called it "uniformly gorgeous and powerful even when subdued," praising how she reins in her pop impulses. It is a borderline but real example of an indie-pop artist reaching toward country/Americana textures rather than a country record proper.
Mitski.lineage: Splits off Americana and country folk's spare, string-backed songwriting (adjacent to X1/V21 territory) through Mitski's indie-rock background; the branch stays within her own art-pop catalog rather than feeding the Core scene.

Mo Troper.description: Fifteen all-killer power-pop tracks that pair intellectual rigor with warmth and classic hooks, per Josh Terry, from a Portland songwriter whose own tagline calls his style 'the Conker's Bad Fur Day of power pop.'
Mo Troper.lineage: Direct descendant of the Big Star/Teenage Fanclub power-pop lineage, part of the 2020s power-pop revival alongside Sharp Pins and Lawn.

Mo Troper.description: Mo Troper's scrappy, hook-crammed debut packs thirteen songs of GBV-scaled power pop into a lo-fi thirty minutes, full of pop-culture non-sequiturs (Judy Garland, Star Wars) delivered with a snotty, deadpan sneer. Pitchfork called its attitude 'snot-nosed pwnage,' which is the point.
Mo Troper.lineage: Sits squarely in the Guided by Voices/Beulah four-track power-pop tradition that runs into the 2010s Portland DIY scene.

Mo Troper.description: Troper's fifteen-song second album sharpens Beloved's melodic instincts into a decade-end favorite for some critics, trading some of the lo-fi scrappiness for slightly cleaner hooks while keeping the rapid-fire, hyper-referential songwriting intact. It rarely lets a song run past two minutes.
Mo Troper.lineage: Continues the GBV-indebted power-pop songwriting of Beloved, tightening the hooks in a way that anticipates Natural Beauty's more melodic turn.

Mo Troper.description: Recorded after failed stints in LA and New York, Troper's third album swaps the earlier records' snottiness for plainer, more durable storytelling, anchored by the Kinks-indebted 'Jas From Australia' about a teenage internet romance. NPR called it 'grinningly great power-pop.'
Mo Troper.lineage: A more melodically direct turn from Troper's earlier GBV-style scrappiness, closer to the Kinks and Teenage Fanclub end of the power-pop lineage.

Modern Baseball.description: A Philadelphia band's breakout emo-revival record, all conversational, self-deprecating lyrics and twin-vocalist trade-offs over fast, hooky guitar pop. A defining document of the mid-2010s emo revival's college-scene sound.
Modern Baseball.lineage: A 2010s emo-revival descendant of the American Football/Promise Ring lineage within X6, part of the same wave that fed the twangy emo crossover of Core lane C9.

Modest Mouse.album: This Is a Long Drive for Someone with Nothing to Think About
Modest Mouse.description: Modest Mouse's debut full-length pairs Isaac Brock's cracked, half-shouted vocals with jittery, start-stop guitar figures and long, meandering song structures built around road-trip imagery and small-town alienation. It is rawer and more overtly punk than the band's later work, closer to a nervous, rural cousin of Pavement's sprawl. The record established the trio's reputation as one of the odder, more promising bands to come out of Up Records' Pacific Northwest roster.
