Modest Mouse.lineage: Modest Mouse's debut on Seattle's Up Records, drawing on the same Pacific Northwest indie underground as Built to Spill and Modest Mouse's own later major-label work.

Modest Mouse.description: A sprawling double-length statement about suburban sprawl eating the rural West, The Lonesome Crowded West pairs Isaac Brock's yelped, half-sung vocals with dynamic shifts from quiet, twangy passages to full-throttle noise on songs like 'Trucker's Atlas' and 'Cowboy Dan.' It remains the definitive Modest Mouse album for many fans, capturing the band's regional preoccupations before they signed to a major label. Its loose, road-worn structure mirrors its subject matter directly.
Modest Mouse.lineage: The high point of Modest Mouse's Up Records period, widely regarded as the clearest statement of the Pacific Northwest strain of 1990s slacker rock before the band's jump to Epic for The Moon & Antarctica.

Modest Mouse.description: Modest Mouse's major-label debut trades some of the earlier records' rawness for more spacious, atmospheric production, with Isaac Brock's lyrics turning toward existential and cosmic themes on '3rd Planet' and 'The Stars Are Projectors.' It is a more deliberately composed, less sprawling record than The Lonesome Crowded West, but keeps the same unsettled, cracked-voice intensity. The album is widely considered the band's artistic peak and the bridge into their 2000s mainstream breakthrough.
Modest Mouse.lineage: Modest Mouse's first album for Epic Records after building a following on Up Records, carrying the band's 1990s Pacific Northwest indie-rock sound into a more polished, widescreen 2000s register.

Moe Bandy.album: I Just Started Hatin' Cheatin' Songs Today
Moe Bandy.description: Bandy's breakthrough single and album title track is a hard-honky-tonk answer song to years of Nashville countrypolitan gloss, sung in a plain, unadorned drawl over Telecaster and steel guitar rather than strings. It set him up, alongside contemporaries like Gene Watson and Vern Gosdin, as part of a 1970s traditionalist pushback against the smoother sound George Jones and Tammy Wynette's producer Billy Sherrill had popularized. The record's blunt, self-aware title says plainly what the whole album delivers.
Moe Bandy.lineage: Part of a mid-1970s traditionalist honky-tonk pushback (alongside Gene Watson and Vern Gosdin) against Nashville's countrypolitan mainstream, a direct precursor to the neo-traditionalist and new-outlaw scenes covered in V7 and V19.

Moe Bandy.description: A concept-adjacent follow-up built around Bandy's own former career as a competitive rodeo rider before he turned to music full-time, the title track using rodeo-clown imagery as a metaphor for heartbreak and public humiliation. The band stays in the same lean, hard-honky-tonk mode as his debut, avoiding string sections entirely. It's a solid second stop in the traditionalist wing of 1970s Nashville that Bandy, Gene Watson, and others represented.
Moe Bandy.lineage: Continues Bandy's traditionalist honky-tonk stance from his debut, drawing directly on his pre-music career as a professional rodeo rider for its central metaphor.

Mojave 3.description: Formed by Neil Halstead and Rachel Goswell after shoegaze act Slowdive was dropped by Creation, Mojave 3's debut trades that band's wall of guitar noise for hushed, pedal-steel-inflected country-folk played at a near-stationary pace. Halstead's soft voice often blends into Goswell's for close, breathy harmonies over spacious, unhurried arrangements. It is one of the clearest examples of a shoegaze band pivoting directly into slowcore's quiet, country-adjacent register rather than dream pop's wash of noise.
Mojave 3.lineage: A direct pivot from classic UK shoegaze (Slowdive) into hushed, pedal-steel slowcore, tying the American sadcore lineage to the British dream-pop scene it drew from.

Mojave 3.description: Mojave 3's second album keeps the pedal steel and close vocal harmonies of the debut but opens the arrangements up a little, with more prominent strings and a slightly warmer production. The pacing stays unhurried throughout, closer to a slow country ballad than to anything resembling the band's shoegaze origins. It solidified Mojave 3's reputation as one of the few UK bands working convincingly in the same hushed, country-tinged register as their American slowcore peers.
Mojave 3.lineage: Deepens Mojave 3's move from shoegaze into pedal-steel-laced slowcore, part of a small but real transatlantic exchange between the American genre and its British sympathizers.

Mojo Nixon and Skid Roper.description: A stripped-down San Diego duo, Mojo Nixon on guitar and holler and Skid Roper on upright washboard and percussion, cut this debut of manic, joke-cracking country-punk with titles like "Jesus at McDonald's." It is closer to novelty rockabilly-punk than to the Blasters' reverent traditionalism, but its raw, homemade recording and country-blues foundation put it squarely in the wider cowpunk orbit. The duo's confrontational, satirical streak became a signature of the San Diego scene.
Mojo Nixon and Skid Roper.lineage: Recorded in the same San Diego scene that produced the Beat Farmers, sharing Enigma Records with Tex & the Horseheads and the Screamin' Sirens; its comic, roots-punk voice anticipated later novelty-adjacent Americana acts.

Mojo Nixon and Skid Roper.description: The duo's second album keeps the same stripped-down guitar-harmonica-washboard setup and rapid-fire, joke-heavy country-punk songwriting, tightening the performances from the debut without smoothing off any of the rough edges. Mojo Nixon's holler and pop-culture-baiting lyrics stayed the band's calling card, a comic, confrontational strain of cowpunk distinct from the more earnest LA and Austin bands. It kept the duo's cult reputation building toward the following year's breakthrough, Bo-Day-Shus!!!.
Mojo Nixon and Skid Roper.lineage: Continues directly from the 1985 debut, part of the same Enigma-Records San Diego cowpunk cluster as the Beat Farmers and Tex & the Horseheads.

Molly Hatchet.description: Molly Hatchet's debut pushes Jacksonville Southern rock toward boogie-metal territory, with producer Tom Werman favoring loud triple-guitar riffing and Danny Joe Brown's shouted, hard-rock vocal delivery over the jazzier improvisation of the Allmans or Marshall Tucker Band. 'Gator Country' and 'Dreams I'll Never See,' a cover of an Allman Joys-era Gregg Allman song, tie the record back to the genre's roots even as the guitars get heavier and the songs get shorter. It became one of the best-selling Southern rock debuts of the late 1970s, arriving just as the genre's first generation was winding down.
Molly Hatchet.lineage: Formed in Jacksonville in the wake of Skynyrd's success, Molly Hatchet represents the harder, more metal-adjacent direction Southern rock guitar bands took as the genre moved into the arena-rock era of the late 1970s and early 1980s.

Molly Tuttle.description: Tuttle's first album with her band Golden Highway (and first for Nonesuch) won the Grammy for Best Bluegrass Album, its guest list (Margo Price, Billy Strings, Old Crow Medicine Show, Gillian Welch) mapping the current bluegrass-and-Americana overlap. Co-produced with dobro player Jerry Douglas, it keeps virtuosic flatpicking guitar at its center while writing personally about growing up different in a small bluegrass town. It is for hearing bluegrass's current critical and commercial high point.
Molly Tuttle.lineage: A 2020s culmination of the same newgrass lineage running from New Grass Revival through Nickel Creek, directly collaborating with Billy Strings and Old Crow Medicine Show as peers in the current bluegrass revival.

Monsters of Folk.description: A studio supergroup pairing Will Johnson's labelmate-adjacent circle with Conor Oberst, Jim James, and M. Ward, 'Monsters of Folk' is a friendly, eclectic indie-folk record that charted in the Billboard Top 20, far more polished and pop-minded than anything in the Molina/Johnson catalog proper. Tracks range from full-band folk-rock ('Say Please') to hushed acoustic duets. It sits closer to 2000s roots-inflected indie than to the Crazy Horse-scale sound of the Magnolia circle.
Monsters of Folk.lineage: Connects Will Johnson to the wider 2000s roots-indie scene around Bright Eyes, My Morning Jacket, and M. Ward, a lighter and more commercial cousin of his work in Centro-matic and with Molina.

Morgan Wallen.description: A sprawling 30-song double album mixing bro-country hooks, hip-hop-adjacent production, and hard-country balladry, Dangerous became the best-selling album (of any genre) of 2021 in the US, propelled by Wallen's rasping East Tennessee drawl. It is loud, maximalist mainstream country built to dominate streaming as much as radio. It is for hearing where bro-country's commercial machinery had arrived a decade after Florida Georgia Line's debut.
Morgan Wallen.lineage: The commercial endpoint of the bro-country lineage running from Jason Aldean and Florida Georgia Line, now scaled to streaming-era volume and genre-blending with hip-hop and pop; Luke Combs runs parallel to Wallen as the more traditionalist mainstream-country pole of the same moment.

Mount Eerie.description: Phil Elverum retired the Microphones name for this three-part, self-recorded meditation on mountains, weather, and mortality, keeping the same homemade production but pushing the songs toward longer, more ambient stretches. Whispered vocals and simple acoustic figures are wrapped in tape hiss, field recordings, and sudden noise passages built entirely in Elverum's own space. It marks the direct, self-produced continuation of the Microphones' home-recording method under a new name.
Mount Eerie.lineage: The album on which Phil Elverum renamed the Microphones as Mount Eerie, carrying the same self-built K Records home-taping method forward into his long-running solo project.

Mount Moriah.description: Heather McEntire and Jenks Miller's Durham band's debut pairs McEntire's Southern-gospel-schooled voice with pedal steel and understated, country-leaning arrangements. It grew out of North Carolina's DIY punk scene, giving the band's country turn an unusually documented, self-aware edge.
Mount Moriah.lineage: Formed by musicians from North Carolina punk and metal bands (McEntire from Bellafea, Miller from Horseback), consciously turning toward country and gospel forms.

Mount Moriah.description: The band's Merge Records debut fills out its country-gospel sound with a fuller band and clearer production, keeping McEntire's plainspoken, often queer-themed lyrics at the center. It marks the point where the band's songwriting caught up with its ambitions.
Mount Moriah.lineage: A fuller-band, Merge Records-backed refinement of the sound introduced on the self-titled debut.

Mountain Man.description: The debut from this Vermont trio of Amelia Meath, Alexandra Sauser-Monnig and Molly Sarle is almost entirely unaccompanied voice, three-part harmonies stacked over minimal or no guitar, drawing directly on old-time Appalachian singing traditions. It is one of the starkest, most purely vocal records in the whole lane, closer to field-recording austerity than to studio folk-pop. A key document for listeners who want the close-harmony end of the indie-folk revival at its most extreme.
Mountain Man.lineage: Rooted directly in old-time Appalachian a cappella and shape-note singing, later a documented influence on Meath's more electronic work in Sylvan Esso, showing how far the folk-revival's vocal tradition could travel.

Mudhoney.description: A six-song fuzz-pedal manifesto that essentially invented grunge's sound before Nirvana existed, all Stooges-worship distortion and slacker sneer. Mark Arm's yowl and the wall of fuzz made this Sub Pop's founding artistic statement.
Mudhoney.lineage: The true ground-zero record of the Seattle line (X8), growing directly from the noise-rock/underground scene of V16 without ever crossing into the Core's twang.

Mumford & Sons.description: The London band's debut defined the stomp-clap-folk sound proper: banjo strum building to shouted group choruses, quiet-to-loud dynamics borrowed as much from indie rock as from folk revival, on hits like 'Little Lion Man' and 'The Cave.' It is unapologetically anthemic, built for festival main stages rather than folk clubs. It is for hearing the single most influential template of the 2010s festival-folk boom.
Mumford & Sons.lineage: Takes the festival-Americana energy Old Crow Medicine Show and the Avett Brothers had been building in the US and turns it into a globally exportable UK indie-folk formula, directly inspiring the Lumineers and the entire stomp-clap-folk wave of the early 2010s.

My Bloody Valentine.description: My Bloody Valentine's debut full-length trades their earlier jangle-pop for tremolo-bent, detuned guitars smeared into a single churning mass, with Bilinda Butcher and Kevin Shields' vocals buried as texture rather than lead instrument. It set the template — pitch-bending 'glide guitar,' whispered non-lyrics, drums mixed almost flat — that every shoegaze band after it copied. For listeners who want to hear the style before Loveless perfected it.
My Bloody Valentine.lineage: Grows out of Velvet Underground/Jesus and Mary Chain noise-drone (the V29 line) crossed with C86 jangle; leads directly to Loveless and the entire shoegaze/dream-pop vocabulary that countrygaze borrows textures from, not toward V29's deadpan songwriting side.

My Bloody Valentine.description: Loveless buries impossibly detuned, whammy-bar-warped guitars, cooing dual vocals and a hidden pop core under layers of tape manipulation and studio experimentation that reportedly bankrupted Creation Records. It is the field guide's canonical entry for the guitar-wall vocabulary — the 'noise wall' and 'harmonized guitars' descriptors — that countrygaze bands filter through pedal steel decades later. Essential listening for anyone tracing where the fuzz-and-drone side of the atlas gets its sonic palette.
My Bloody Valentine.lineage: The commercial and aesthetic peak of the C86/shoegaze branch off V29's drone lineage; its guitar-wall production directly informs the noise/slowcore Context lane and, at a distance, the pedal-steel-and-fuzz textures of Core countrygaze bands like Wednesday.

My Morning Jacket.description: Jim James's Louisville band's debut was recorded in a converted grain silo, drenching every guitar and vocal in natural reverb to create a hazy, spectral take on Southern rock and country-soul. It set the reverb-soaked signature sound the band would carry, in refined form, through the rest of its catalog.
My Morning Jacket.lineage: Draws on Neil Young, Crazy Horse and classic Southern rock, filtered through the natural echo of the silo where the band recorded, a sound that would define My Morning Jacket's whole career.

My Morning Jacket.description: A more melodic, song-focused record than the debut, still soaked in the grain-silo reverb but with clearer hooks, including the epic slow-build closer 'Strangulation!'. It began building the band's reputation as a formidable live act.
My Morning Jacket.lineage: Refines the reverb-heavy Southern rock of 'The Tennessee Fire' into tighter, more melodic songwriting.

My Morning Jacket.description: The album that broke the band nationally, opening with the horn-driven 'Mahgeetah' and stretching out into extended Southern-rock jams like 'Run Thru' and 'Dancefloors'. It is the fullest expression of the band's early reverb-soaked, jam-friendly sound before Jim James began streamlining things.
My Morning Jacket.lineage: The culmination of the reverb-drenched Southern rock built up across the first two records, and the album that connected the band to the wider jam and indie circuits alike.

My Morning Jacket.description: With a mostly new lineup, the band traded some of the Southern-rock haze for reggae-tinged rhythms, synths and tighter songcraft, broadening its sound without losing Jim James's falsetto or the band's love of a big chorus. It is often cited as the moment My Morning Jacket became an arena-scale indie band rather than a cult one.
My Morning Jacket.lineage: A deliberate widening of the reverb-soaked Southern rock of 'It Still Moves' toward more varied, radio-friendly songcraft.

My Morning Jacket.description: An intentionally scattershot record that jumps from falsetto funk to prog-rock guitar workouts to straight country balladry, dividing longtime fans but confirming the band's refusal to repeat itself after 'Z'. Its title track and the itchy funk of 'Highly Suspicious' are as far from the band's reverb-soaked debut as it ever traveled.
My Morning Jacket.lineage: Pushes the genre-hopping widened out on 'Z' even further, absorbing funk and prog alongside the band's Southern-rock and country roots.

My Morning Jacket.description: Recorded back home in Louisville in a converted gymnasium, this record pulled the band back toward its reverb-heavy Southern-rock roots after the detours of 'Evil Urges', with the title track's marching-band middle section standing as one of Jim James's most ambitious arrangements.
My Morning Jacket.lineage: A conscious return to the Louisville-recorded, reverb-soaked sound of the band's earliest records after the genre experiments of 'Evil Urges'.

My Morning Jacket.description: Written during Jim James's breakup with a longtime partner, this is a warmer, more consistently melodic record than 'Evil Urges', cut at Stinson Beach in California rather than Louisville. It reads as the band settling into a reliable, mature version of its sound.
My Morning Jacket.lineage: A late-period continuation of the widened, more melodic sound the band settled into after 'Z', now filtered through James's breakup songwriting.

NE-HI.description: A kinetic Chicago DIY debut mixing jangly, interlocking guitar lines with garage-rock urgency, part of what Terry calls one of Chicago indie rock's best two-LP runs.
NE-HI.lineage: Descends from Flying Nun/Feelies jangle crossed with garage-rock energy, rooted in Chicago's DIY venue scene.

NE-HI.description: The second half of NE-HI's acclaimed two-album run, with sharper songwriting and more melodic hooks layered over the same jangly, fuzz-toned guitar interplay.
NE-HI.lineage: Continuation of NE-HI's jangle/garage-rock songwriting within Chicago's DIY scene.

Naked Prey.description: Former Green on Red drummer Van Christian's Tucson band play rough-edged desert country-rock, and this third album leans on well-chosen covers, a driving take on the Rolling Stones' 'Silver Train' and a sparse, haunted reading of Glen Campbell's 'Wichita Lineman,' to carry songs whose own hooks don't always match David Seger's wiry, urgent guitar work. It captures the same Arizona/California desert-rock axis as Giant Sand, with a harder, more amphetamine-punk edge. Christian's rough, weathered voice fits the band's tired-highway subject matter.
Naked Prey.lineage: Formed by Green on Red's original drummer Van Christian after he relocated from Los Angeles to Tucson, Naked Prey shared the California/Arizona 'desert rock' axis with the Dream Syndicate and Giant Sand.

Nanci Griffith.description: An album of folk and country songs Griffith did not write but loved, Other Voices, Other Rooms is a covers record with an all-star guest list (Bob Dylan, Emmylou Harris, Iris DeMent, John Prine, Guy Clark) built around plain, warm acoustic arrangements. It works as a listening guide to the folk-revival and Texas songwriter tradition she came out of, tracing a direct line from Townes Van Zandt and Woody Guthrie through her own generation. It won the Grammy for Best Contemporary Folk Album.
Nanci Griffith.lineage: A tribute to the Texas and folk-revival songwriters (Townes Van Zandt, Woody Guthrie, Ian Tyson) who shaped Griffith's own writing, explicitly mapping the lineage this whole lane traces.

Nanci Griffith.album: Once in a Very Blue Moon
Nanci Griffith.description: Recorded in Nashville with bluegrass players Béla Fleck and Mark O'Connor alongside guest harmonies from a then-unknown Lyle Lovett, this is the album where Griffith's folk beginnings fully absorbed a country and bluegrass backbone. The title track and Roseville Fair (a Bill Staines cover) run on fingerpicked acoustic guitar, banjo rolls and fiddle rather than the sparser sound of her first two records, while her clear, slightly nasal Texas voice keeps the songs grounded in plainspoken storytelling. It is generally treated as the record where her mature style, folk songwriting dressed in acoustic country-bluegrass clothes, first clicked into place.
Nanci Griffith.lineage: Bridges Griffith's Austin folk beginnings with the Nashville session-player world, and Lyle Lovett's guest vocal here is a direct, documented link between two of this lane's core artists.

Nanci Griffith.album: The Last of the True Believers
Nanci Griffith.description: Griffith's fourth album, cut with largely the same Nashville pickers as Once in a Very Blue Moon, pushes further into full-band country-folk arrangement while keeping her clear-diction, front-porch storytelling intact. Love at the Five and Dime (later a hit for Kathy Mattea) sketches a whole small-town marriage in under four minutes, the kind of concrete, novelistic detail that runs through the whole record. It earned her first Grammy nomination and is often cited as the clearest statement of her 1980s folk-into-country period before she moved toward a more mainstream Nashville sound on Lone Star State of Mind.
Nanci Griffith.lineage: Continues the Nashville-session, acoustic-country-folk direction of Once in a Very Blue Moon, and "Love at the Five and Dime" became a standard covered across Nashville, spreading Griffith's plainspoken storytelling well beyond the folk circuit.

Nanci Griffith.album: There's a Light Beyond These Woods
Nanci Griffith.description: Nanci Griffith's self-released debut, cut for a tiny Austin label while she was still working as a kindergarten teacher, is spare acoustic-folk songwriting sung in her light, girlish voice, closer to the John Denver/Judy Collins folk tradition than to the rowdier progressive-country records around her. Song titles about small-town Texas life and quiet coming-of-age moments set the template for everything she recorded afterward. It sold only regionally at the time but is now treated as the first chapter of one of the era's most acclaimed folk-country careers.
Nanci Griffith.lineage: The starting point of Griffith's career inside the Austin folk scene that also nurtured Lyle Lovett and Robert Earl Keen; her plainspoken, small-town storytelling runs in a direct line from Guy Clark's example.

Nap Eyes.description: Nigel Chapman's conversational, half-spoken vocals ride over loose, unhurried jangle-rock guitar, closer to Jonathan Richman or Silver Jews than most of their slacker-rock peers. Bookish, philosophical lyrics over simple, warm arrangements.
Nap Eyes.lineage: Descends from the deadpan funny-sad songwriting line (Silver Jews/Drag City) crossed with VU-descended jangle guitar; the start of one of the decade's most consistent guitar-rock runs.

Nap Eyes.description: A more assured, road-tested version of the band's talky jangle-rock, with Chapman's lyrics turning toward philosophy and self-doubt over bright, ringing guitar lines.
Nap Eyes.lineage: Continuation of the band's Silver Jews/VU-descended jangle songwriting.

Nap Eyes.description: A slightly more polished, full-band record that keeps the band's signature talk-singing but adds more melodic hooks and confident guitar solos.
Nap Eyes.lineage: Third album in Nap Eyes' jangle/talk-song lineage, moving toward a bigger label and wider audience.

Nap Eyes.description: Nap Eyes' most direct, hook-forward record, still built on Chapman's conversational delivery but with brighter, more confident arrangements.
Nap Eyes.lineage: Continues the band's jangle/talk-song lineage into a fourth album.

Nap Eyes.description: Per Josh Terry, this album pairs the band's conversational, bookish lyrics with sunny organ and strong guitar work; he calls Nap Eyes one of the decade's best guitar-rock bands.
Nap Eyes.lineage: Latest chapter in Nap Eyes' Silver Jews/VU-descended jangle lineage.

Nashville West.description: Taped by Gene Parsons at a 1968 club gig, this is the only recorded document of the short-lived quartet he formed with Clarence White, Gib Guilbeau and Wayne Moore, playing hot instrumental country and rockabilly before any of them had joined the Byrds or Flying Burrito Brothers. It sat unreleased for a decade before Sierra put it out in 1978. As a prehistory document it is essential to understanding where the genre's key session players came from, even though it postdates the band itself by ten years.
Nashville West.lineage: A recording of the pre-Byrds, pre-Burritos band that trained several of this lane's key players (Clarence White, Gene Parsons, Gib Guilbeau) in hot country picking before they scattered into the Byrds, Flying Burrito Brothers and Swampwater.

Natalie Jane Hill.description: Hill's debut, recorded live at an Atlanta studio: intricate, self-taught fingerpicking under a plainspoken, nature-fixated songwriting voice indebted to Michael Hurley and Karen Dalton.
Natalie Jane Hill.lineage: Grew out of Hill's move to the Blue Ridge Mountains and immersion in the American Primitive fingerstyle scene, opening onto her fuller-band later records.

Natalie Jane Hill.description: A transitional second record, recorded to 8-track with producer Jason Chronis, that opens Hill's solo fingerstyle sound to a small circle of collaborators including Mat Davidson.
Natalie Jane Hill.lineage: Follows Azalea as Hill moved back to Austin, expanding her palette ahead of the full-band Hopeful Woman.

Natalie Jane Hill.description: Recorded live in Texas and Western North Carolina with Mat Davidson's pedal steel and flute throughout, Hill's third LP is her most fleshed-out, twang-forward record yet.
Natalie Jane Hill.lineage: Josh Terry flagged it as an album-of-the-year contender for its full-band arrangements; continues Hill's fingerstyle-folk lineage into pedal-steel-laced country-folk.

Nathan Salsburg.description: Salsburg, the curator of the Alan Lomax Archive, brings a folklorist's ear for old-time and British Isles melody to his own fingerstyle playing on this debut, favoring warm, major-key tunes over drone or raga abstraction. The picking is clean and unshowy, closer to a folk-song arranger's sensibility than to Fahey's more experimental side. It established No Quarter, run by Salsburg's wife Joan Shelley's label partners, as a home for melodic, tradition-steeped instrumental guitar.
Nathan Salsburg.lineage: Grew out of Salsburg's day job archiving Alan Lomax's field recordings, channeling old-time and British Isles folk melody through the Fahey-descended solo-guitar format, and helped establish No Quarter as a hub for the style alongside Cian Nugent.

Nathan Salsburg.album: Hard for to Win and Can't Be Won
Nathan Salsburg.description: Salsburg's second album sharpens the melodic, tradition-conscious approach of Affirmed, its titles and tunes drawing directly on the old-time and British ballad sources he works with at the Lomax Archive. The playing stays warm and unhurried, prioritizing clear melody over technical flash or drone. It is one of the gentlest, most straightforwardly pretty records in the post-Fahey guitar revival.
Nathan Salsburg.lineage: Continues Salsburg's folklorist approach to solo guitar, sitting alongside Glenn Jones's old-time-inflected records as part of the 2010s revival's gentler, melody-first wing.

Nathan Salsburg.description: As its plain title suggests, Third is Salsburg settling further into his own voice, six-string and twelve-string pieces that keep the melodic clarity of his first two records while stretching a few pieces out into longer, more exploratory territory. It shows a guitarist increasingly comfortable departing from strict folk-tune structure without losing the warmth that defines his playing. The record rounds out what is generally considered his strongest run of solo albums.
Nathan Salsburg.lineage: Completes Salsburg's initial trilogy of folk-song-rooted solo guitar records, part of the same No Quarter and Louisville circle that includes his frequent collaborator James Elkington.

Nathaniel Rateliff & the Night Sweats.description: After a career in quieter folk music, Rateliff reinvented himself with a horn section and Stax-style soul-revival energy on 'S.O.B.,' a stomp-and-shout single that became a festival-circuit anthem far bigger than his earlier solo folk records. It swaps banjo strum for horns and gang vocals but keeps the same communal, crowd-participation energy as the rest of this lane. It is for hearing the soul-revival cousin of stomp-clap folk's festival-anthem instinct.
Nathaniel Rateliff & the Night Sweats.lineage: Shares the same festival-crowd, singalong-anthem instinct as Mumford & Sons and the Lumineers but channels it through horn-driven Stax soul rather than banjo folk, an adjacent branch of the big-tent Americana mainstream.

National Photo Committee.description: Chicago's National Photo Committee plays raucous, country-tinged bar rock, with spidery pedal steel lines cutting through gravelly, shouted vocals. Its songs favor an unresisting, rowdy energy over polish, closer to a loud honky-tonk stage than a studio. A record built to be heard live.
National Photo Committee.lineage: Part of the same Chicago DIY-country circle as Tobacco City and Red PK, connecting the city's cowpunk-adjacent bar-rock scene to the wider Bandcamp alt-country revival.

Neil Michael Hagerty.description: Royal Trux co-founder Neil Hagerty's first outing under his own name, released the same year he produced Bill Callahan's Woke on a Whaleheart, is a loose, riff-driven solo record that keeps the classic-rock damage of Royal Trux's later albums without Jennifer Herrema's co-lead vocals. It is a minor entry mostly of interest to listeners tracing Hagerty's connections to the Drag City deadpan circle through his production work. Not deadpan-country itself, but part of the same label ecosystem.
Neil Michael Hagerty.lineage: Documents Hagerty's solo work in the same period he began producing for Bill Callahan, part of the wider Drag City-adjacent circle even though released on Domino.

Neil Young.description: Young's first solo album is a lush, string-and-woodwind-laden folk-rock record, closer to Jack Nitzsche's orchestral arrangements than to the ragged band sound he would soon build with Crazy Horse. Songs like 'The Loner' and 'The Old Laughing Lady' already carry his strange, reedy phrasing even under all the studio polish. Young was reportedly unhappy with the original mix for years, but the record set out the moody, wandering songwriting he'd spend the next decade refining.
Neil Young.lineage: Young's solo launch straight out of Buffalo Springfield, still wearing 1960s orchestral-pop production before Crazy Horse stripped the sound down.

Neil Young.description: Young's second solo album is the true beginning of this lane: his first record with Danny Whitten, Billy Talbot and Ralph Molina as Crazy Horse, cut fast and loose after the orchestral polish of the debut. 'Cinnamon Girl,' 'Down by the River' and 'Cowgirl in the Sand' were reportedly written in a single feverish afternoon, and the two long tracks stretch out into raw, one-note guitar solos that became Young's signature. It is the blueprint for every long, fuzzy, half-in-tune guitar jam that follows in this lane.
Neil Young.lineage: The founding document of the Neil Young/Crazy Horse sound, with Danny Whitten's rhythm guitar setting the template that feeds everything from Zuma through Ragged Glory to Wednesday and MJ Lenderman decades later.

Neil Young.description: Recorded mostly at Young's home studio with a shifting cast including Stephen Stills and a very young Nils Lofgren on piano, this is the quiet, high, cracked-voice side of Young's writing: 'Only Love Can Break Your Heart,' 'Tell Me Why,' and the title track's strange, apocalyptic imagery over simple piano chords. 'Southern Man' is the record's one loud detour, a fuzzy electric protest song that Lynyrd Skynyrd would later answer. It set the template for the acoustic, plainspoken side of Young that keeps resurfacing across his catalog.
Neil Young.lineage: Young's move from Crazy Horse's electric sprawl to hushed piano-and-guitar songwriting, a direct ancestor of the folk side of this whole lane and of records like Harvest and Comes a Time.

Neil Young.description: Young's commercial peak, cut partly in Nashville with the Stray Gators (Ben Keith's pedal steel is all over it) and partly with a full orchestra in London for 'A Man Needs a Maid' and 'There's a World.' 'Heart of Gold' went to number one and made Young a reluctant star, something he'd spend the rest of the decade running from. It is the most straightforwardly pretty record in this catalog, the country-folk side of the lane at its most polished.
Neil Young.lineage: The commercial high point of Young's country-folk side, cut with the same Nashville pedal-steel band sound as Harvest Moon two decades later; its success is the thing Tonight's the Night and On the Beach deliberately reject.

Neil Young.description: Recorded live on the disastrous, drug-strained 1973 tour that followed Harvest's success, with a band that barely rehearsed the new songs before playing them to arenas expecting more 'Heart of Gold.' None of these songs were ever released in studio versions, which makes the record feel like a document of a breakdown in real time, all ragged edges and cracked high notes. It is the first record of what fans call Young's 'ditch trilogy,' turning hard away from the polish that made him famous.
Neil Young.lineage: The opening record of Young's self-described 'ditch trilogy,' made in direct, panicked reaction to Harvest's mainstream success and pointing straight at On the Beach and Tonight's the Night.

Neil Young.description: The second leg of the ditch trilogy, cut fast with a loose, murky mix that Young reportedly favored over cleaner takes because it matched the mood. 'Revolution Blues' is a menacing, almost spoken-word song written in the voice of a Manson-like cult leader, while the closing 'Ambulance Blues' rambles for close to nine minutes over a simple acoustic figure. It is one of the bleakest, least commercial records Young ever released on a major label, and it is exactly the record Harvest's audience did not want.
Neil Young.lineage: The middle of the 'ditch trilogy,' recorded in deliberate retreat from Harvest's success and sharing its hungover, unpolished mood with Tonight's the Night, recorded around the same period.

Neil Young.description: A patchwork record stitched from several different sessions, pairing rowdy honky-tonk numbers cut with a country band (Emmylou Harris sings harmony on several tracks) with a leftover Crazy Horse cut and the solo acoustic 'Will to Love.' The mismatched sequencing gives it a loose, tossed-off feel, but 'Like a Hurricane,' with its long, droning guitar solo over a wash of organ, is one of Young's most enduring live staples. It sits right at the crossroads of the country and Crazy Horse sides of this lane.
Neil Young.lineage: A grab-bag that sums up the whole V20 project in one record: honky-tonk duets with Emmylou Harris on one side, a distorted Crazy Horse epic on the other.

Neil Young.description: A warm, mostly acoustic country-folk record built around close vocal harmonies with Nicolette Larson, who duets on much of the album. It was reportedly remixed at the last minute after Young decided the original mix was too polished, adding a rougher acoustic guitar overdub across the whole thing to knock some of the shine off. It is the gentlest record between Zuma and Rust Never Sleeps, closer in spirit to Harvest than to Crazy Horse.
Neil Young.lineage: The clearest bridge between Harvest's Nashville-pop side and Harvest Moon a decade and a half later, with Nicolette Larson's harmonies doing what Emmylou Harris's did on American Stars 'n Bars.

Neil Young.description: A brief, patchwork record split between leftover mellow acoustic songs from the mid-1970s and a handful of new, flag-waving country tunes recorded quickly in 1980, including the title track's blunt, almost jingoistic patriotism. It runs under 30 minutes and reads more like a transitional sketch than a statement, but it previews the political directness Young would return to on records like Living with War. Critics were divided on the political turn at the time, and it remains one of his more argued-over records.
Neil Young.lineage: A minor, transitional record that shows Young's country-folk side turning overtly political, a mood he'd revisit decades later on Living with War.

Neil Young.description: Young's strangest detour, built around vocoder-processed vocals and synthesizers, made in part while trying to find a way to communicate with his nonverbal son, who used a computer-assisted communication device. It confused his label and audience at the time and kicked off a string of genre-hopping records that led Geffen to sue him for making 'uncharacteristic' music. Heard now, it plays like an outsider new-wave record more than a Crazy Horse album, but it belongs in this lane as proof of how far Young was willing to stretch the sound.
Neil Young.lineage: The most electronic record in Young's catalog, made during his Geffen years and directly responsible for the label's lawsuit over 'non-commercial' music; a strange cousin to the drum-machine and synth experiments elsewhere in indie music's country-adjacent fringes.

Neil Young.description: A straight-up Nashville country record, cut with a band that included Waylon Jennings and Willie Nelson on guest vocals, pedal steel and fiddle throughout, closer to outlaw country than anything else Young made. It was the last and most fully-realized of the Geffen genre detours, and it briefly made Young a presence on the country charts. It is a minor record in his catalog but a real data point for how directly this lane touches outlaw and honky-tonk country.
Neil Young.lineage: Young's most straightforward country record, cut with Waylon Jennings and Willie Nelson, connecting this lane directly to outlaw country's Nashville mainstream.

Neil Young.description: A harsh, drum-machine-and-synth-driven rock record that Young himself later called one of his worst, made during his least-loved commercial period. It has little of the loose Crazy Horse feel; the production is cold, digital and very mid-1980s, with Young's voice pushed into a shouted upper register on songs like 'Hippie Dream.' It is included here mainly as a completionist marker of how far this artist could stray from the sound this lane is built around, and how he'd claw his way back with Life and Freedom.
Neil Young.lineage: The commercial and critical low point of Young's 1980s wandering, directly preceding his return to Crazy Horse on Life the following year.

Neil Young.description: A horn-driven blues-and-R&B record, cut with a touring big band called the Bluenotes, built around the title track's blunt swipe at rock stars doing beer and soda commercials. MTV initially banned the video for using unlicensed Michael Jackson and Whitney Houston imagery before reversing course and giving it Video of the Year. It's an outlier in this catalog stylistically, more bar-band blues than Crazy Horse fuzz, but it's part of the same restless, contrarian streak that runs through his whole Geffen-Reprise return era.
Neil Young.lineage: One of Young's genre-hopping detours back at Reprise, swapping Crazy Horse's guitars for a horn section, but sharing the same blunt, contrarian political streak as Living with War almost twenty years later.

Neil Young.description: Young's comeback record after a wandering decade, bookended by acoustic and electric versions of 'Rockin' in the Free World,' the song that became his signature protest anthem for the next thirty years. The record mixes solo acoustic tracks with full-band, occasionally Crazy Horse-adjacent noise, and it was widely received as Young reclaiming his own sound after the Geffen years. It set up the next decade of alternating loud and quiet records that defines this whole lane.
Neil Young.lineage: The record where Young reclaims his own template after a decade of genre experiments, its acoustic/electric 'Rockin' in the Free World' bookends echoing Rust Never Sleeps a decade earlier.

Neil Young.description: A deliberate, twenty-years-later sequel to Harvest, reuniting most of the same Stray Gators musicians (Ben Keith's pedal steel again central) for a warm, mostly acoustic country-folk record. It arrived at the height of grunge, an unfashionable, unhurried move that ended up connecting with a huge audience anyway and going platinum. Songs like 'Unknown Legend' and 'From Hank to Hendrix' explicitly look backward, tying the whole catalog's threads together in real time.
Neil Young.lineage: A direct, self-aware sequel to Harvest with the same Nashville-pedal-steel band, showing the country-folk half of this lane at its most comfortable and popular.

Neil Young.description: Young's MTV Unplugged set, recorded acoustic (though not entirely unplugged, an electric pump organ and other quiet electric touches slip in) with a small band including Nicolette Larson and Ben Keith, reworking songs from across his catalog including a stripped-down 'Like a Hurricane.' It's one of the more purely pretty documents of the acoustic, country-folk side of this lane, sequenced almost like a career overview. It remains one of the more fondly remembered entries in MTV's Unplugged series.
Neil Young.lineage: A career-spanning acoustic overview that puts the quiet, country-folk half of Young's catalog (Harvest, Comes a Time, After the Gold Rush) side by side in one set.

Neil Young.description: Young backed by Pearl Jam rather than Crazy Horse, cut live off the floor in a handful of days with almost no overdubs, the raw production leaving songs ending in unplanned feedback and count-offs. Eddie Vedder sings lead on one track ('Peace and Love'), and the whole record sounds like a grunge-era update of the Ragged Glory formula with a younger band supplying the muscle. It is the clearest single document of Young's direct hand in shaping the sound of the bands he'd influenced.
Neil Young.lineage: Young backed by Pearl Jam instead of Crazy Horse, making explicit the influence line running from Ragged Glory into 1990s grunge.

Neil Young.description: A quiet, largely acoustic record built from songs Young had been sitting on for years, some dating back to the Harvest Moon and Unplugged era, with Ben Keith's pedal steel again anchoring the sound. It is gentle almost to a fault, closer in spirit to Comes a Time than to anything loud, arriving as a deliberate change of pace after the noisier Year of the Horse. 'Daddy Went Walkin'' and 'Distant Camera' show Young turning reflective and domestic as he moved into his fifties.
Neil Young.lineage: A late entry in the quiet, pedal-steel-driven country-folk lineage running from Harvest through Comes a Time and Harvest Moon.

Neil Young.description: Recorded in Nashville shortly before eye surgery for a brain aneurysm, with Emmylou Harris singing harmony and a return to the pedal-steel, string-and-banjo arrangements of Harvest and Harvest Moon. Songs like 'Far from Home' and 'This Old Guitar' are openly reflective about mortality and family history, giving the record a valedictory feel even though Young recovered fully. It closes out what fans sometimes call his 'Harvest trilogy,' the third and gentlest chapter after Harvest and Harvest Moon.
Neil Young.lineage: The third chapter of what fans call Young's 'Harvest trilogy,' again featuring Emmylou Harris and the same pedal-steel country-folk sound as the other two.

Neil Young.description: A fast, blunt protest record against the Iraq War and the Bush administration, cut in about two weeks with a 100-voice choir and a trumpet player standing in for a guitar solo on several tracks. 'Let's Impeach the President' is as direct as protest songwriting gets, naming its target outright over a driving rock arrangement. It's one of the most overtly political records in his catalog, continuing a streak of topical songwriting that runs back through Ohio and Southern Man.
Neil Young.lineage: A blunt-force protest record in the direct lineage of 'Ohio' and 'Southern Man,' Young's political songwriting turned all the way up against the Iraq War.

Neil Young.description: A sequel in name only to the long-bootlegged, unreleased 1977 Chrome Dreams, mixing a gospel choir on 'The Believer,' a horn-driven soul number, and the sprawling, eighteen-minute guitar showcase 'Ordinary People' (a song Young had been sitting on since the 1980s). It's a genuinely varied record, jumping between styles more than most of his 2000s output, and 'Ordinary People' in particular became a favorite among longtime fans for how far it stretches the Crazy Horse-style guitar solo. It shares only a title with the real Chrome Dreams, which wouldn't see official release for another sixteen years.
Neil Young.lineage: A stylistic grab-bag that borrows its name from the legendary unreleased 1977 Chrome Dreams while extending the long-solo, horn-and-choir experiments of Young's mid-2000s work.

Neil Young.description: A stark solo-electric record produced by Daniel Lanois, who wrapped Young's guitar and voice in loops, echo and dub-style processing rather than a full band, so the record sounds like Crazy Horse's fuzz distilled down to just one guitar and a room full of reverb. Songs like 'Hitchhiker' and 'Love and War' are largely just Young alone with his instrument, made huge and strange through Lanois's studio treatment. It won a Grammy nomination and stands as one of the more unusual late-career reinventions of the raw, distorted sound this lane is built around.
Neil Young.lineage: A radical solo reduction of the 'Crazy Horse fuzz' sound, one guitar and Daniel Lanois's studio treatments standing in for the whole band.

Neil Young.description: Recorded solo acoustic in Toronto in January 1971, right between After the Gold Rush and Harvest, and held in the vault for 36 years before its release as the first entry in Young's Archives Performance Series. It captures early, unreleased versions of 'Old Man' and 'Heart of Gold' months before they appeared on Harvest, along with cuts from After the Gold Rush played solo on guitar and piano. As a between-albums snapshot of the quiet, country-folk half of Young's sound at its most intimate, it's one of the most treasured entries in his archival series.
Neil Young.lineage: An archival release (recorded 1971, released 2007) capturing Young solo and acoustic between After the Gold Rush and Harvest, with early versions of songs that would define both records.

Neil Young.description: Drawn from six solo shows at a small Washington, D.C. club in late 1970, this archival release captures Young alone on guitar and piano just before Harvest, including an early solo reading of 'Old Man' cut before the song had a full-band arrangement. It's a quieter, more intimate companion to Live at Massey Hall 1971, recorded only weeks apart, and it fills in another piece of the gap between After the Gold Rush and Harvest. Being a small-club document rather than a concert-hall one, it has an even closer, more conversational feel between songs.
Neil Young.lineage: An archival release (recorded 1970, released 2013) from the same solo-acoustic period as Live at Massey Hall 1971, filling out the picture of Young between After the Gold Rush and Harvest.

Neil Young.description: A long-shelved 1974-75 album about the end of Young's relationship with actress Carrie Snodgrass, pulled from the release schedule at the last minute in favor of the harsher Tonight's the Night and left in the vault for 45 years. Musically it sits between those two records, mostly acoustic and quietly devastated rather than drunk and howling, with early versions of songs like 'Star of Bethlehem' that later turned up elsewhere. Young himself has called it the 'missing link' between Harvest, Comes a Time and Harvest Moon, and its long-delayed release closed one of the most famous gaps in his catalog.
Neil Young.lineage: An archival release (recorded 1974-75, released 2020) that Young himself calls the missing link between Harvest and Harvest Moon, shelved originally in favor of the harsher Tonight's the Night.

Neil Young.description: A single-session solo acoustic album cut in one night in August 1976, with Young running through early, spare versions of songs that would later appear (in very different, full-band arrangements) on American Stars 'n Bars, Rust Never Sleeps and other later records. Producer David Briggs's minimal, close-mic'd recording leaves in studio chatter and the sound of Young tuning between takes. Released 41 years later, it works almost like a Rosetta Stone for a whole stretch of Young's mid-70s songwriting, showing the bare acoustic bones under songs fans knew only in their electric Crazy Horse forms.
Neil Young.lineage: An archival release (recorded 1976, released 2017) showing the solo-acoustic origins of songs later reworked with Crazy Horse on American Stars 'n Bars and Rust Never Sleeps.

Neil Young.description: One of rock's most famous unreleased albums, assembled as an acetate in 1977 from sessions dating back to 1974 and widely bootlegged for decades before Young finally issued it officially. It mixes solo acoustic tracks with full-band Crazy Horse cuts, including early versions of songs (like 'Powderfinger' and 'Like a Hurricane') that fans had only known from their later official releases elsewhere. Many critics over the years argued it would have been one of Young's very best records had it come out on schedule, and the belated 2023 release let listeners finally judge that claim directly.
Neil Young.lineage: An archival release (recorded 1974-77, released 2023) of one of the most legendary unreleased albums in rock history, sitting at the source of songs later spread across American Stars 'n Bars, Comes a Time and Rust Never Sleeps.

Neil Young.description: Another long-shelved album from the extremely prolific 1974-77 stretch, mixing relaxed acoustic songs with a loose, countryish backing band, sitting alongside Homegrown and the official Chrome Dreams as one more piece of the vault Young spent the 2020s finally opening. Several of its songs had already surfaced elsewhere in different versions, so this release functions mainly as a snapshot of how they were originally sequenced and arranged. It's a minor entry next to Homegrown or Chrome Dreams, but it rounds out a remarkably clear picture of just how much material Young was sitting on during that period.
Neil Young.lineage: An archival release (recorded 1977, released 2025) from the same prolific mid-70s vault as Homegrown and Chrome Dreams, filling in yet another piece of that period's songwriting.

Neil Young and Crazy Horse.description: Recorded in 1973 but held back for two years, this is Young's grief record for two friends who died of heroin overdoses: Crazy Horse guitarist Danny Whitten and roadie Bruce Berry. The band reportedly drank heavily before takes, and the vocals are shredded, off-key, barely holding together on songs like the title track and 'Tired Eyes.' It is the rawest, least polished record in this catalog, more a wake caught on tape than a finished album, and it set the standard for how ugly and honest a Crazy Horse record could sound.
Neil Young and Crazy Horse.lineage: Young's bleakest Crazy Horse-adjacent record, made in mourning for Danny Whitten; its ragged, barely-in-control sound is the direct ancestor of the lo-fi, live-in-the-room ethic this whole atlas keeps returning to.

Neil Young and Crazy Horse.description: Crazy Horse's first record after Danny Whitten's death, with Frank 'Poncho' Sampedro joining on rhythm guitar, a lineup that would stay together for decades. The nine-minute 'Cortez the Killer' is the centerpiece, a slow-building, single-note lead guitar showcase that became one of the most covered and cited Young performances ever. After two bleak ditch-trilogy records, Zuma sounds like the band finding its footing again, still ragged but warmer and more open.
Neil Young and Crazy Horse.lineage: The record where the classic four-piece Crazy Horse lineup (Young, Talbot, Molina, Sampedro) locks into place, the direct template for Ragged Glory, Sleeps with Angels and every Crazy Horse album since.

Neil Young and Crazy Horse.description: Split cleanly down the middle, side one solo acoustic and side two full-volume Crazy Horse, the record bookends itself with 'My My, Hey Hey (Out of the Blue)' and its electric twin 'Hey Hey, My My (Into the Black),' the songs that gave punk-era Young the line 'it's better to burn out than to fade away.' 'Powderfinger,' a narrative death ballad, sits at the album's emotional center. Assembled from a 1978 tour with a stage set built to look like giant amps and roadies dressed as hooded 'road-eyes,' it is Young's most theatrical statement of the two sides of his sound.
Neil Young and Crazy Horse.lineage: The record that most explicitly states this lane's whole thesis, an acoustic folk side and a distorted Crazy Horse side on one LP, cited for decades by punk and grunge musicians as proof Young never went soft.

Neil Young and Crazy Horse.description: The full-length concert document of the same 1978-79 tour that produced Rust Never Sleeps, pairing solo acoustic renditions with extended, feedback-drenched Crazy Horse jams on 'Cortez the Killer' and 'Like a Hurricane.' It captures the theatrical stage show (giant amps, road crew dressed as Jawa-like 'road-eyes') and remains one of the most-cited live rock albums of its era. As a document of the band actually stretching out in real time, it is arguably the purest recorded evidence of the Crazy Horse jam at full length.
Neil Young and Crazy Horse.lineage: The concert-length companion to Rust Never Sleeps, showing the acoustic/electric split of that record played out live at length.

Neil Young and Crazy Horse.description: A blunt, repetitive, almost mechanical Crazy Horse record, written while Young was consumed with his son's cerebral palsy and reportedly using rhythmic repetition in the songs to mirror the patterning therapy the family was doing at home. 'T-Bone' repeats basically one line ('got mashed potatoes, ain't got no T-bone') for nine minutes over a churning riff. It's one of the least song-oriented, most purely textural records in the catalog, closer to proto-noise-rock than anything else Young made in this period.
Neil Young and Crazy Horse.lineage: The most repetitive, riff-obsessed Crazy Horse record, foreshadowing the noise and drone experiments Young would return to on Arc a decade later.

Neil Young and Crazy Horse.description: Crazy Horse's return after a decade away from a Neil Young studio record, though the 1980s production (gated drums, synth pads) still sits oddly over the band's usual raw sound. 'Mideast Vacation' and 'Long Walk Home' carry blunt political commentary, part of a Reagan-era run of protest songs. It's a transitional, imperfect record, but it's the hinge between the lost Geffen years and the band's full-force comeback on Ragged Glory three years later.
Neil Young and Crazy Horse.lineage: Crazy Horse's return to a Neil Young studio album after Re-ac-tor, still burdened by 80s production but pointing the way back to the raw sound of Ragged Glory.

Neil Young and Crazy Horse.description: Recorded live off the floor in a barn at Young's ranch, with the band reportedly playing full takes twice a day without repeating a song, this is Crazy Horse at maximum volume and maximum sprawl, several tracks running past ten minutes of distorted, barely-in-tune guitar interplay. It landed right as grunge was breaking, and bands like Pearl Jam and Sonic Youth (who opened Young's tour behind it) cited it as proof the old guard could still out-loud the new one. It is the clearest single-album distillation of the 'Crazy Horse fuzz' descriptor this whole lane is built around.
Neil Young and Crazy Horse.lineage: The Crazy Horse album most directly cited by the grunge generation as proof of Young's continuing relevance, a direct influence on Dinosaur Jr., Sonic Youth and the whole 1990s noisy-guitar underground.

Neil Young and Crazy Horse.description: A double live album from the Ragged Glory tour, cut at the height of grunge with Sonic Youth opening, capturing Crazy Horse at its loudest and most extended, with 'Like a Hurricane' and 'Cortez the Killer' both stretching well past ten minutes. It was originally packaged with the companion noise collage Arc, sold together as a way of framing feedback itself as part of the performance. It's the sound of an older band matching, and arguably out-muscling, the young noise-rock bands built in its image.
Neil Young and Crazy Horse.lineage: The live document of the Ragged Glory tour, recorded as grunge broke and directly informing that scene's embrace of extended, feedback-heavy guitar rock.

Neil Young and Crazy Horse.description: A 35-minute collage of feedback, amp hum and song fragments edited together from the Ragged Glory tour's between-song noise, originally sold packaged with the live album Weld. It has almost no conventional songwriting on it at all, just texture, drone and distortion, making it Young's most explicitly avant-garde release. Sonic Youth's Thurston Moore has cited it as a key noise-rock touchstone, a strange, unlikely handshake between a 1960s folk-rock veteran and the noise underground he was touring alongside.
Neil Young and Crazy Horse.lineage: Young's pure noise experiment, assembled from Ragged Glory tour feedback and cited by Sonic Youth and the noise-rock underground as proof of his standing in that scene.

Neil Young and Crazy Horse.description: Recorded in the shadow of Kurt Cobain's death (Cobain had quoted 'it's better to burn out than to fade away' in his suicide note), this is a hushed, mournful, occasionally still very loud Crazy Horse record, split between quiet dirges and the sprawling closer 'Change Your Mind.' The mood is heavier and more grief-stricken than Ragged Glory, closer in spirit to Tonight's the Night's wake-like atmosphere. It is one of the most purely emotionally weighted records in the whole catalog.
Neil Young and Crazy Horse.lineage: A grief record shadowed by Kurt Cobain's death and his quotation of Young's own lyric, closing a loop between Young's influence on grunge and grunge's cost.

Neil Young and Crazy Horse.description: A loose, sometimes shambolic Crazy Horse record, closing with a lo-fi bar-recording of 'Music Arcade' captured on a handheld tape recorder at an actual Bay Area bar. It leans further into deliberate rawness than even Ragged Glory, with long, meandering solos on 'Big Time' and 'Slip Away' that sound closer to a rehearsal tape than a finished master. Critics were split on the record's shagginess at the time, but it has aged into a favorite among Young obsessives for exactly that unfinished quality.
Neil Young and Crazy Horse.lineage: Crazy Horse pushing deliberate looseness even further than Ragged Glory, its lo-fi bar-tape closer a small, direct ancestor of the DIY-recording ethic prized elsewhere in this atlas.

Neil Young and Crazy Horse.description: A live album (and companion Jim Jarmusch concert film) from the 1996 Broken Arrow tour, leaning into long, loose, sometimes shaggy extended jams rather than tight renditions. Jarmusch's accompanying black-and-white film was shot in deliberately gritty, unglamorous 16mm, matching the record's rough-edged mood. It's a minor entry compared to Weld or Live Rust, valued mostly by committed fans for how far the band was willing to stretch songs in concert.
Neil Young and Crazy Horse.lineage: A shaggier companion to Weld, capturing Crazy Horse's mid-90s live sound and its ongoing appeal to filmmakers and musicians drawn to its unpolished, in-the-room feel.

Neil Young and Crazy Horse.description: A concept record and accompanying film telling a loose, multi-generational story about a fictional California town called Greendale, sung mostly in character and stretched out with long, repetitive Crazy Horse jams under the narrative. It's one of the most overtly storytelling-driven records in Young's catalog, closer to a folk opera than a normal album, touching on media, the environment and small-town life. Reception was divided at the time, but it has become a cult favorite for how far it pushes the 'ragged guitar plus plainspoken story' idea that runs through this whole lane.
Neil Young and Crazy Horse.lineage: Young's most explicit storytelling concept record, extending the narrative instincts of Broken Arrow's suite-writing into a full small-town saga with Crazy Horse's fuzz underneath.

Neil Young and Crazy Horse.description: A covers record reworking old folk standards and songbook staples ('Oh Susannah,' 'Clementine,' 'This Land Is Your Land') as full-volume Crazy Horse jams, treating nursery-rhyme-familiar songs like they were unreleased Ragged Glory outtakes. It's a strange, funny, sometimes genuinely unsettling record, closing with an extended, mostly instrumental take on 'God Save the Queen' repurposed as 'America the Beautiful.' It reunited the classic Crazy Horse lineup for the first time in years and set up the same-year Psychedelic Pill.
Neil Young and Crazy Horse.lineage: Old-time American folk songs run through the Crazy Horse fuzz machine, tying this lane's Crazy Horse sound directly back to the pre-1965 folk roots the whole atlas traces to.

Neil Young and Crazy Horse.description: A sprawling double album recorded right after Americana with the same reunited Crazy Horse lineup, opening with the 27-minute jam 'Driftin' Back,' one of the longest tracks Young ever released. It's the fullest, most unhurried expression of the Crazy Horse fuzz-and-feedback sound in his late catalog, songs given room to wander for ten or twenty minutes at a stretch rather than being trimmed for radio. Critics generally received it as the strongest Crazy Horse studio album since Sleeps with Angels.
Neil Young and Crazy Horse.lineage: The 2010s peak of the classic four-piece Crazy Horse sound, letting the band's long-solo instincts run further than almost any record since Ragged Glory.

Neil Young and Crazy Horse.description: Crazy Horse's first studio album in seven years and the first to feature Nils Lofgren on guitar in place of the retired Frank Sampedro, recorded high in the Rockies at a home studio. It splits between long, fuzzy jams ('She Showed Me Love' stretches past thirteen minutes) and gentler, more overtly environmentalist songwriting. It reads as a late-career reaffirmation of the classic sound after Young's mostly solo and archival 2010s output.
Neil Young and Crazy Horse.lineage: The reunion record that brought Nils Lofgren, who first played with Young back on After the Gold Rush, into the Crazy Horse guitar chair.

Neil Young and Crazy Horse.description: Recorded live off the floor inside a restored 1870s log barn high in the Colorado Rockies, using the room's natural echo instead of studio reverb, this is Crazy Horse leaning fully into the 'live in the room' ethic that's run through their records since Ragged Glory. It won the Grammy for Best Rock Album, an unusual honor this late in Young's career, and was accompanied by a documentary film of the sessions. Songs like 'Song of the Seasons' mix accordion into the usual guitar-heavy mix, giving the record a slightly rustic, campfire edge.
Neil Young and Crazy Horse.lineage: A late-period return to the barn-recorded, live-off-the-floor method Young and Crazy Horse first used on Ragged Glory three decades earlier.

Neil Young and Crazy Horse.description: Produced by Rick Rubin and recorded live to analog tape, this Crazy Horse record leans into environmental and personal themes across loose, warm arrangements, including some unusual instrumental pairings Rubin pushed the band toward. It's less about volume than mood, a mellower late-period Crazy Horse record than Barn or Colorado, closer in spirit to the reflective side of Harvest Moon than to Ragged Glory's roar. It continued the string of Crazy Horse albums the reunited, Lofgren-era lineup put out through the early 2020s.
Neil Young and Crazy Horse.lineage: A Rick Rubin-produced late-period Crazy Horse record, mellower than Barn or Colorado but continuing the same reunited lineup's run of 2020s albums.

Neil Young and Crazy Horse.description: Recorded in 2000-01 during the breakup of Young's first marriage and shelved for two decades in favor of the brighter Are You Passionate?, this is a moody, atmospheric Crazy Horse record that Young himself has described as foggy, blue and desolate. It's quieter and more restrained than most Crazy Horse records, closer in mood to Sleeps with Angels or Tonight's the Night than to Ragged Glory's roar. Its long-delayed 2022 release let a genuinely dark chapter of the band's history finally see daylight.
Neil Young and Crazy Horse.lineage: An archival release (recorded 2000-01, released 2022) documenting a somber Crazy Horse session shelved for two decades, closer in mood to Sleeps with Angels than to the band's louder records.

Neil Young and Crazy Horse.description: An archival collection of 1969 recordings by the original Crazy Horse lineup (Danny Whitten, Billy Talbot, Ralph Molina) with producer Jack Nitzsche on piano, drawn from the same sessions that produced Everybody Knows This Is Nowhere. It includes alternate takes and songs left off that record, offering a wider window into the band's first year together before Whitten's death three years later. For a lane built around this lineup's guitar interplay, it's a direct look at the moment the sound was first invented.
Neil Young and Crazy Horse.lineage: An archival release (recorded 1969, released 2024) documenting the founding Crazy Horse lineup around the sessions for Everybody Knows This Is Nowhere.

Neil Young and the Chrome Hearts.description: Young's first album with a new backing band, the Chrome Hearts (Micah Nelson on guitar, Spooner Oldham on keys, plus a rhythm section), formed after Crazy Horse guitarist Nils Lofgren stepped back and continuing the same ragged, plainspoken songwriting the whole lane is named for. Opener 'Family Life' and the pointed protest song 'Big Change' show the band settling into the role Crazy Horse has played for over fifty years, distorted guitar and blunt political lyrics side by side. It's the newest entry in a lineage that now runs an unbroken six decades back to Buffalo Springfield.
Neil Young and the Chrome Hearts.lineage: A new backing band, the Chrome Hearts, stepping into the role Crazy Horse has occupied since 1969, keeping the ragged-guitar/cracked-voice sound going into a new decade.

Neil Young and the Shocking Pinks.description: A short, deliberately retro rockabilly pastiche, cut with a new backing band (the Shocking Pinks) doing 1950s-style slap-bass and doo-wop harmonies, clocking in under 25 minutes. It was another entry in the run of genre experiments that prompted Geffen's lawsuit against Young for delivering music 'unrepresentative' of his usual sound. It's a minor, oddball record, but it shows the same restlessness that runs through Trans and Old Ways, Young refusing to repeat himself even at commercial cost.
Neil Young and the Shocking Pinks.lineage: Part of Young's contrarian early-80s run of genre exercises for Geffen, sandwiched between the synth-pop of Trans and the straight country of Old Ways.

Neil Young and the Stray Gators.description: A concert recording from the same troubled 1973 tour documented (with a different, later lineup) on Time Fades Away, but capturing an earlier show with the original Harvest touring band, the Stray Gators, including Ben Keith's pedal steel. It's a calmer, more together-sounding document than Time Fades Away, closer to how Harvest's songs were meant to sound live before the tour fell apart. Released decades later as part of the Archives series, it works as a companion piece showing the tour's earlier, steadier chapter.
Neil Young and the Stray Gators.lineage: An archival release (recorded 1973, released 2019) from the same Time Fades Away tour, but with the original Stray Gators lineup, showing the country-rock side of that period before it frayed.

Neil Young with Crazy Horse.description: A secret November 2023 club show at Toronto's tiny Rivoli, where Crazy Horse played Ragged Glory front to back for an audience of a few hundred, released the following spring as a Record Store Day live album with songs retitled from lyric fragments. It's a loose, sweaty, low-stakes document, the opposite of an arena spectacle, and it plays like the band checking in on a thirty-four-year-old record to see if the fuzz still holds up. It does.
Neil Young with Crazy Horse.lineage: A full live run-through of Ragged Glory more than three decades later, the same lineup revisiting the album most identified with the 'Crazy Horse fuzz' sound.

Neko Case.description: Case's debut with Her Boyfriends is a straight-up honky-tonk record, cut fast in Vancouver with a rockabilly-leaning backing band and covers alongside her own songs. It predates the more gothic, image-driven songwriting she became known for, closer to a bar band's Saturday-night set than a studio statement. It shows the traditional-country grounding she would later bend into stranger shapes.
Neko Case.lineage: An early document of Case's move from punk drumming into honky-tonk singing, made before she developed the surreal, nature-haunted songwriting of her Bloodshot and Anti- albums.

Neko Case.description: Case's first true solo album puts her powerhouse voice at the center of noir-tinged country songs about jealousy, violence, and small towns, backed by Her Boyfriends' twangy, reverb-drenched guitars. It is rawer and more directly country than what followed, closer to the Bloodshot roster around her than to the art-pop she would develop on Anti-. 'Set Out Running' and 'Whip the Blankets' show the widescreen, cinematic imagery that becomes her signature.
Neko Case.lineage: Released on Bloodshot Records alongside labelmates like the Old 97's and Waco Brothers, placing Case squarely in the Chicago insurgent-country scene before she moved toward Anti-'s art-rock audience.

Neko Case.description: A darker, more atmospheric record than the debut, built around slow-burning arrangements, reverb, and desert imagery instead of barroom twang. Case's voice moves between a hushed near-whisper and full-throated wail, and songs like 'Deep Red Bells' turn true-crime dread into widescreen Americana. It marks the turn toward the more art-damaged, less strictly country sound of her later Anti- records.
Neko Case.lineage: The last Case solo record fully on Bloodshot before she signed with Anti-, bridging the label's insurgent-country roster and the more expansive songwriting that followed.

Neko Case.description: A short live album recorded with fellow Bloodshot-adjacent Canadians the Sadies, mixing a few originals with covers of Loretta Lynn and Buffy Sainte-Marie. The Sadies' twangy, reverb-heavy guitar work gives the set a spaghetti-western edge that Case's studio records rarely reach. It captures her as a bandleader in a live room rather than a studio auteur.
Neko Case.lineage: Documents Case's ongoing collaboration with the Sadies, the Toronto band who also backed Jon Langford and other figures in the wider Bloodshot-adjacent alt-country network.

Neko Case.description: Case's first album for Anti- trades linear narrative for fragmented, almost folkloric songwriting, full of foxes, hospitals, and half-told stories set to spare, orchestral country-pop arrangements. 'Star Witness' and 'Hold On, Hold On' pair some of her most direct melodies with lyrics that read like dream logic. It is widely treated as the record where her singular songwriting voice fully arrived.
Neko Case.lineage: Case's move to Anti- expanded her audience beyond the insurgent-country scene without abandoning pedal steel and drawl, becoming a touchstone for the 2000s wave of literary alt-country songwriters.

Neko Case.description: A bigger, more orchestrated record than its predecessor, built around themes of nature reclaiming the human world and closing with a 31-minute recording of crickets. 'This Tornado Loves You' and 'People Got a Lotta Nerve' show Case at her most anthemic, backed by a huge cast of guest musicians. It became her highest-charting album and pushed her further from strict alt-country into orchestral art-pop.
Neko Case.lineage: Extends the widescreen songwriting of Fox Confessor into more maximalist territory, cementing Case as one of the era's defining voices to come out of the Bloodshot-to-Anti- alt-country pipeline.

Neko Case.album: The Worse Things Get, the Harder I Fight, the Harder I Fight, the More I Love You
Neko Case.description: A darker, more personal record written in the aftermath of her mother's death and her own struggles, mixing horn-driven arrangements with some of her bleakest lyrics. 'Man' reworks gender expectations into a defiant anthem, while other songs turn inward toward grief and anger. It keeps the widescreen production of Middle Cyclone while pulling the songwriting closer to confession.
Neko Case.lineage: Continues Case's Anti- run of increasingly personal, orchestrated songwriting, distinct from but indebted to the twangier records that launched her out of the Bloodshot scene.

Neko Case.description: Case's most sonically adventurous record folds synths and dense orchestration into her country-rooted songwriting, with lyrics addressing climate anxiety, autobiography, and myth side by side. 'Bad Luck' and the title track show her stretching further from twang than ever while keeping her voice as the anchor. It was recorded in the years after a house fire destroyed her Vermont home, which colors the record's unsettled tone.
Neko Case.lineage: The furthest extension yet of the art-rock direction Case took after leaving Bloodshot, still carrying the alt-country DNA of her early records in its storytelling and vocal delivery.

Neko Case.description: Case's most recent album continues the confessional turn of her 2010s work, released alongside a memoir covering similar ground, with 'Wreck' among its more directly autobiographical songs. It keeps the string-laden, widescreen arrangements of Hell-On while easing back toward more spacious, vocal-forward production. Reviewers have read it as a summing-up record for a songwriter now decades removed from her insurgent-country beginnings.
Neko Case.lineage: The latest chapter of Case's post-Bloodshot Anti- catalog, still tracing back to the twangy songwriting that first got her grouped with the 2000s alt-country scene.

Neu Blume.description: A Detroit duo's warm, crisp midtempo jangle record, built around layered melodies and unvarnished lyricism, with pedal steel coloring several tracks. Per Josh Terry, it stakes out its own lane of graceful, inviting jangle-pop.
Neu Blume.lineage: Descends from the DIY jangle/college-radio line (Big Star, Flying Nun) filtered through 2020s Midwest indie rock.

Neutral Milk Hotel.description: Jeff Mangum's first Neutral Milk Hotel album was largely recorded and mixed by Robert Schneider on homemade equipment, layering fuzzed-out horns, tape hiss, and Mangum's strained, urgent voice over songs like 'Song Against Sex' and 'Naomi.' The production is thick and murky by design, closer to a bedroom collage than a conventional studio rock record, even as the songwriting reaches for big, surreal images. It set up the more fully-realized concept-album leap of 'In the Aeroplane Over the Sea' two years later.
Neutral Milk Hotel.lineage: Jeff Mangum's debut as Neutral Milk Hotel within the Elephant 6 collective, built with the same four-track, homemade production ethos as labelmates Olivia Tremor Control and Apples in Stereo, and the direct lead-in to 'In the Aeroplane Over the Sea.'

Neutral Milk Hotel.album: In the Aeroplane Over the Sea
Neutral Milk Hotel.description: Recorded quickly with Robert Schneider in a home studio, 'In the Aeroplane Over the Sea' wraps Jeff Mangum's raw, straining voice and surreal, Anne Frank-haunted lyrics in fuzzed horns, singing saw, and distorted acoustic guitar that never resolves into clean production. Songs like 'Holland, 1945' and the title track push from hushed verses into blaring, brass-choked climaxes within seconds. Despite selling modestly on release, it became the most influential Elephant 6 record and a founding text of American indie lo-fi's second wave.
Neutral Milk Hotel.lineage: The culmination of Neutral Milk Hotel and the wider Elephant 6 collective's homemade recording ethic, recorded in the same lo-fi, Beach Boys-indebted tradition as Apples in Stereo and Olivia Tremor Control and enormously influential on the next two decades of indie folk and lo-fi songwriting.

New Grass Revival.description: The debut of the band that coined the term 'newgrass,' fusing traditional bluegrass instrumentation (banjo, mandolin, fiddle) with rock and jazz-influenced improvisation and a hippie-era openness to extended jamming. It broke from bluegrass orthodoxy's strict traditionalism far more aggressively than contemporaries like the Osborne Brothers. It is for hearing bluegrass's founding progressive-jam experiment, decades before Billy Strings.
New Grass Revival.lineage: Descends directly from the first-generation bluegrass tradition (Bill Monroe, the Stanley Brothers, documented in this lane's parent R1) but breaks from its strict traditionalism to found the 'newgrass' style, opening the improvisational, genre-blending path that Nickel Creek, Punch Brothers, and Billy Strings all eventually walk.

New Riders of the Purple Sage.album: New Riders of the Purple Sage
New Riders of the Purple Sage.description: Formed as a Bay Area country-rock side project with Jerry Garcia on pedal steel and Grateful Dead drummer Mickey Hart behind the kit, the New Riders' debut runs through John Dawson's outlaw and stoner-cowboy songs like Henry, Portland Woman and the minor hit Glendale Train. Garcia's pedal steel, twangy and unhurried, is the record's defining sound, right before he left the band to focus on the Dead full time and was replaced by Buddy Cage. It is the only New Riders studio album to feature him, making it the clearest bridge between the two bands' rosters.
New Riders of the Purple Sage.lineage: Born directly out of the Grateful Dead's Bay Area circle, with Garcia and Hart on the record and bassist Dave Torbert soon joining from the same scene; the New Riders extended the Dead's own country turn into a dedicated band that toured as the Dead's regular opening act for years.

New Riders of the Purple Sage.description: The New Riders' second album, made after Buddy Cage replaced Garcia on pedal steel, leans harder into honky-tonk and rockabilly covers, Hello Mary Lou, Willie and the Hand Jive, alongside Dawson and Marmaduke's own drinking and trucking songs like the title-setting Dim Lights, Thick Smoke (And Loud, Loud Music). Cage's steel playing is faster and twangier than Garcia's had been, pushing the band's sound closer to straight honky-tonk than to the Dead's psychedelic country.
